title: Rescuing an Existing Project
text:
Triage sequence

Freeze and preserve the current state; do not silently overwrite inputs or outputs.
Inventory files, scripts, data locations, access constraints, environments, and recent results.
Ask the previous owner or stakeholders what is trusted, provisional, or broken.
Reconstruct the smallest defensible path from an input to a named result.
Record gaps as risks and choose a stopping point for rescue work.
Create a handoff note before making major changes.







Important



Unlabeled cleanup can erase provenance. Keep a dated rescue log and preserve the original state when permissions and storage allow.

title: Minimum GeoEpi Project Standard
text:
Proposed draft policy — review required



This page proposes a minimum standard. It is not approved policy. Institutional, legal, contractual, privacy, security, records-management, funder, and data-governance requirements take precedence.

title: Minimum GeoEpi Project Standard
text:
1. Purpose
The minimum standard makes GeoEpi projects understandable, reviewable, reproducible where access permits, and transferable across people and time. A requirement belongs here only when failure materially threatens scientific defensibility, data security, result traceability, project continuity, collaboration, publication, operational use, handoff, or preservation.

title: Minimum GeoEpi Project Standard
text:
2. Scope
Apply this standard to active GeoEpi research, surveillance, field-data, software, modeling, simulation, operational, and HPC projects. Apply it proportionally to exploratory work and legacy projects. It covers project records and workflows, not scientific conclusions or a single software stack.

title: Minimum GeoEpi Project Standard
text:
3. Guiding principle
The GeoEpi Lab Book is a living resource. The minimum is a floor for defensibility and continuity, not a rigid template for every project. Use Required for universal controls, Conditionally required when project characteristics trigger a control, Recommended for practices that improve quality but are not universal, and Optional for useful local choices.
The required artifacts describe information that must be retained and discoverable. They do not necessarily require separate files. A README, configuration file, rendered report, workflow manifest, validated dataset, or automated log may satisfy multiple requirements when the information is clear, durable, and traceable. Separate formal records become necessary when project complexity, risk, contributors, operational importance, or institutional requirements justify them.

title: Minimum GeoEpi Project Standard
text:
4. Definitions

Source data: received or collected data preserved without undocumented modification.
Derived data: data created by a documented transformation from source or staged data.
Consequential: capable of changing a reported result, operational action, data protection, or project handoff.
Result traceability: the ability to identify inputs, code, parameters, environment, execution, and output for a result.
Authoritative location: the project location designated as current for a specified artifact or workflow.
Project artifact: a durable record needed to understand, execute, review, release, hand off, or close a project.

title: Minimum GeoEpi Project Standard
text:
5. Universal minimum requirements

Project identity — Required
Every active project must identify a stable title or identifier, project lead, primary analytical or data-management contact, research or operational objective, intended outputs, audience or decision context, current status, and authoritative repository or project location.
Every project must contain a concise scope statement identifying its objective, intended output, owner, authoritative location, and current status. For a small project, the README may contain this scope statement; a separate charter is not universal.


Project README — Required
Every active project must have a current project-level README covering purpose, responsible personnel, repository structure, data locations, setup requirements, principal workflows, expected outputs, access restrictions, current status, known limitations, and contact or handoff information. Use templates/project-readme-template.md.


Directory and object organization — Required
Separate source data, interim/staged data, derived data, analysis code, configuration, documentation, outputs, logs, and temporary files. Repository-specific names are permitted when their meanings are documented. No universal folder tree is required.


Source-data protection — Required
Preserve source data without undocumented modification. A correction must be reproducible, recorded, attributable, and linked to the corrected or derived version. Do not put protected source data in Git unless authorized.


Data provenance — Required
For each external or internally collected dataset, record a stable local identifier, source, collector/provider, acquisition method and date, original filename or source identifier, version/release date, license or use restriction, a checksum when proportionate, and transformations connecting source to derived data.
When the transformation chain is clear, versioned scripts and their retained outputs may constitute the source-to-derived provenance record; a separate provenance table is conditional.


Data classification and protection — Required
Identify relevant restrictions, such as public, internal, restricted, confidential, personally identifiable, proprietary, governed by a data-use agreement, or sensitive ecological/geographical information. These labels are descriptive until institutional terminology is approved; do not invent USDA or laboratory classification policy.


Metadata and data dictionaries — Required
Document variables, units, data types, identifiers, categories/codes, missing-value conventions, date/time conventions, coordinate reference systems, spatial units, temporal support, and important derivations. Use the data dictionary template where a table is appropriate.


Scripted transformations — Required
Retain consequential transformations and analyses in scripts, workflows, notebooks, or rendered computational documents. A manual step is permitted only when scripting is not reasonable, the procedure and inputs/outputs are documented, the responsible person is recorded, and the effect can be reviewed.


Version control — Required
Use Git-based version control for code and documentation unless a documented exception applies. Git is generally not the correct storage location for credentials, protected data, large raw datasets, sensitive spatial records, temporary files, generated caches, or non-redistributable proprietary material.


Software and computational environment — Required
Record enough environment information to reconstruct the project at a level proportional to risk and complexity. This may include R and package versions, renv.lock, a Python environment, containers, system libraries, external command-line tools, GIS/database versions, HPC modules, and operating-system details. renv is not universal.


Configuration and parameters — Required
Represent consequential paths and parameters explicitly through configuration files, command-line arguments, function arguments, workflow manifests, or documented constants. Major results must not depend solely on undocumented interactive state. A configuration file, workflow manifest, or documented function or command invocation may constitute the parameter record; a separate parameter document is not required when the information is already clear.


Quality assurance — Required
Document checks appropriate to the workflow. Examples include schema, missingness, duplicates, ranges, units, identifiers, temporal consistency, spatial validity, geometry, raster alignment, masks/exclusions, output completeness, model convergence, and simulation completion. Do not impose irrelevant checks. An executable QA script and retained report or log may constitute the QA/QC record when the checks, results, exceptions, and reviewer are discoverable.


Result traceability — Required
Every externally reported or operationally consequential result must be traceable to identified input data, versioned code, relevant configuration and parameters, computational environment, a specific output, and a run identifier or reproducible execution path where appropriate.


Decision documentation — Required
Record consequential decisions in a durable location: exclusion rules, case-definition changes, parameter changes, source substitutions, boundary changes, modeling assumptions, workflow redesigns, and release decisions. Trivial coding choices do not need formal decision records. Git history, issues, pull requests, or a decision log may satisfy this requirement when the decision, rationale, responsible person, and date are recoverable.


Publication or release — Required at external release
Before external release, complete a clean render or workflow execution; document source data; identify code version; synchronize manuscript, code, figures, and tables; provide data/code availability statements; record licenses or restrictions and known limitations; and complete review proportionate to risk and importance. A separate release package or checklist is required only when the release context warrants it.


Handoff and closeout — Required when responsibility changes, work pauses indefinitely, or the project closes
All active projects must avoid undocumented personal dependencies and keep current README, repository, data-location, known-issue, and reproduction information. An actual handoff record is required when responsibility changes. A final closeout record is required when work pauses indefinitely or the project closes; it records access transfer, archive/retention, unfinished work, removal or transfer of personal dependencies, and the authoritative final version.

title: Minimum GeoEpi Project Standard
text:
6. Requirements by project type
These are conditionally required when the project class applies.

Spatial and spatiotemporal projects
Record CRS and datum, coordinate units, extent, resolution or spatial support, raster origin/alignment, spatial mask, boundary source/version, spatial transformations, coordinate uncertainty, and sensitive-location handling. For example, a map can be irreproducible when a boundary release or raster alignment is not recorded.


Epidemiological and surveillance projects
Record case definition and version/effective dates, event/report date meanings, denominator, deduplication, linkage, reporting delays, jurisdictional changes, confidentiality restrictions, and snapshot/extraction date. A changed case definition or delayed report can otherwise make two valid-looking estimates incomparable.


Ecological and field-data projects
Record sampling design and locations, taxonomic identifiers, units, detection limits, observer/instrument, effort, missing observations, and sensor calibration where relevant. Field effort and detection limits can change apparent abundance even when the analysis code is unchanged.


Genomics and phylogenetics projects
Record sample identifiers, sample-to-sequence linkage, accessions, reference genome, database versions, read-processing workflow, filters, alignment, tree-building configuration, metadata joins, and sensitive host/location handling. A sequence alignment without its sample linkage and filtering record is not a transferable input.


Statistical, mathematical, and simulation models
Record model purpose, conceptual structure, variables, parameters and units, initial/boundary conditions, calibration data, validation, stochastic seeds, replicate strategy, scenarios, acceptance criteria, and limitations. A simulation result without seed and scenario definitions cannot be checked or extended.


Operational workflows
Record production schedule, input availability, failure behavior, logging, alerting, retry behavior, output validation, responsible operator, and change control. Operational outputs require an owner who can explain what happened when an input is late or invalid.


HPC workflows
Record submission script, software environment, modules/container, resource request, job identifier, array definition, input manifest, output destination, stdout/stderr logs, failure and retry status, and the relationship between local and cluster environments. Use templates/hpc-run-record-template.yml.

title: Minimum GeoEpi Project Standard
text:
8. Research-lifecycle checkpoints
Each gate is a concise, verifiable checkpoint. A failed gate is recorded and corrected or handled through an exception.

1. Project initiation

Identity, objective, audience, outputs, status, owner, and authoritative location are recorded.
Scope, risks, data restrictions, and likely project type are stated.
README contains the concise scope statement; a standalone charter exists if the project triggers that condition.
Planned data locations and access owners are identified.
Initial environment and workflow approach are recorded.



2. Data intake

Source identifier, provider/collector, acquisition date, original name, version, and restriction are recorded.
Source data are preserved or the reason is documented.
Required metadata and spatial/temporal conventions are available; a separate dictionary exists when warranted.
Source-to-derived plan and checks are identified.
Sensitive or governed data have an approved storage/access decision.



3. Analysis readiness

Inputs, code, configuration, parameters, and environment record are discoverable.
Consequential manual steps and decisions are documented.
QA/QC checks are defined and applicable.
Entry point or execution path is identified.
Expected outputs and completion criteria are stated.



4. Result review

Checks ran and exceptions are recorded.
Reported outputs map to input, code, parameters, environment, and run/output IDs.
Model, simulation, spatial, genomic, or operational diagnostics are reviewed where applicable.
Limitations and unresolved decisions are visible.
A reviewer appropriate to project risk is identified.



5. Publication or operational release

Clean execution or render succeeds.
Code, manuscript, figures, tables, and outputs are synchronized.
Data/code availability, licenses, and access restrictions are stated.
Release review and approval are recorded.
Version, archive, and public/private locations are identified.



6. Handoff when responsibility changes

README and inventory are current.
Access, credentials ownership, and data locations are transferred safely.
Principal-output reproduction steps succeed or limitations are recorded.
Known issues, unfinished work, and next actions are listed.
New responsible roles accept the handoff.



7. Closeout when work pauses indefinitely or ends

Authoritative final version is named.
Archive, retention, and disposal decisions are recorded.
Reproducibility materials and restrictions are preserved.
Undocumented personal dependencies are removed or transferred.
Closeout record and contact for future questions are stored.

title: Minimum GeoEpi Project Standard
text:
9. Proportionality
Documentation and controls scale with project longevity, contributors, data sensitivity, analytical complexity, computational cost, operational importance, publication and regulatory implications, likelihood of handoff, and cost of reconstruction.







Profile
Proportionate minimum




Small exploratory analysis
README containing the concise scope statement, source-data record, scripts, environment note, result traceability, and no separate charter unless another trigger applies


Publication-oriented research
Full data inventory, dependency record, QA/QC documentation, review, release preparation, archive plan, and a standalone charter because publication intent triggers it


Operational or high-consequence workflow
Formal configuration, logging, validation, failure recovery, review authority, controlled releases, and documented ownership



A standalone charter is conditionally required when a project has multiple contributors or organizations, persists beyond a short exploratory period, has external funding or formal deliverables, publication intent, operational use, sensitive or governed data, substantial computational cost, formal handoff expectations, or consequential policy, regulatory, or management use.

10. Exceptions
Use templates/project-exception-record.md. An exception must record the unmet requirement, reason, consequence, compensating control, responsible person, approval authority, review date, and closure status. An exception cannot override legal, contractual, security, privacy, or institutional requirements. Approval authority remains an open policy decision.

text:
13. Evidence base
This proposal combines observed GeoEpi practice in the practice audit with external guidance: The Turing Way, Good Enough Practices in Scientific Computing, TIER Protocol, RDMkit, DataONE, FAIR Principles, FAIR Principles for Research Software, CARE Principles, USDA NAL guidance, CDC Field Epidemiology Manual, FGDC metadata, GBIF georeferencing, Ecological Metadata Language, and Ecological Forecasting Initiative. Access/review date: 2026-08-05.



Standard area
Principal external guidance
GeoEpi evidence
Policy interpretation




Project organization and README
Good Enough Practices; The Turing Way
READMEs and recognizable project entry points recur across the sample.
Require discoverable identity and scope, not a fixed folder tree.


Source-data protection and provenance
RDMkit; DataONE
OSF/archive links and project-specific data assets recur; acquisition and transformation records are inconsistent.
Require source protection and provenance information; separate tables are conditional.


Metadata and data dictionaries
DataONE; Ecological Metadata Language
Data dictionaries and workflow notes appear in some mature projects.
Require understandable variables, units, codes, and spatial/temporal meaning.


Version control and scripted analysis
The Turing Way; Good Enough Practices
Versioned R scripts are present throughout the sample.
Require version control or a documented exception; retain consequential transformations.


Computational environments
The Turing Way; RDMkit
Environment records and lockfiles are uneven; EpiPlume exposes detailed computational configuration.
Require proportional environment information, not one package manager.


QA/QC
The Turing Way; Good Enough Practices
EpiPlume exposes tests and validation scripts; other projects expose fewer formal checks.
Require workflow-appropriate checks; scripts and retained reports may satisfy the record.


Result traceability and reproduction packages
TIER Protocol
Rendered supporting-information sites and OSF archives recur, but run/output inventories vary.
Require traceability for reported or operational results; formal packages are event- or risk-dependent.


Collaboration and decision records
The Turing Way
Project ownership, decisions, and handoff information are not consistently visible.
Require durable consequential decisions; Git history/issues may suffice.


FAIR data
FAIR Principles
External archives and publication links support reuse in several projects.
Use FAIR as an orientation, subject to access and governance constraints.


FAIR research software
FAIR Principles for Research Software
Licenses and citation metadata are inconsistent across repositories.
Recommend reusable licensing and citation; institutional policy remains open.


CARE and responsible governance
CARE Principles
Public repository review cannot establish governance for sensitive or Indigenous data.
Require authority, responsibility, and restrictions to be identified without inventing policy.


Spatial metadata and georeferencing
FGDC; GBIF
Spatial rasters, boundaries, and model domains recur; CRS and uncertainty records vary.
Conditionally require CRS, datum, extent, alignment, provenance, and uncertainty.


Epidemiological data management
CDC Field Epidemiology Manual
Surveillance and outbreak repositories expose model/report workflows but not consistently case-data metadata.
Conditionally require case definitions, dates, denominators, linkage, and snapshots.


Ecological metadata and forecasting
EML; EFI
Ecological and simulation workflows are represented, but forecast records are not uniform.
Conditionally require sampling, measurement, effort, calibration, scenario, and forecast metadata.


Publication and preservation
TIER Protocol; DataONE
Publications, rendered reports, and OSF links recur in several repositories.
Require release readiness and preservation decisions at the relevant event.



Evidence informs this proposal but does not itself establish GeoEpi policy. The proposal uses original prose and flags areas requiring institutional interpretation in Open policy decisions.

title: Validation Plan
text:
Identify candidate results
Record the analysis ID and version, candidate result IDs, input dataset versions, relevant runs, result locations, and readiness limitations carried from Analyze. Do not validate an informal description such as “the final model” without an identifiable analysis version and result.

title: Validation Plan
text:
Define validation questions
Examples include:

Are important assumptions seriously violated?
Are predictions acceptably calibrated for the intended population?
Does the method distinguish higher-risk from lower-risk units where that matters?
Does performance remain acceptable across years or regions?
Are conclusions sensitive to reasonable alternative priors?
Do simulation outputs obey biological or physical constraints?
Are uncertainty intervals appropriate for the stated use?
Does uncertainty change the decision?

title: Validation Plan
text:
Define evidence before reviewing outcomes
The validation plan describes what will be assessed. The validation record contains the authoritative conclusion about whether the candidate results support their stated use. Where practical, record checks, data, grouping or spatial-temporal separation, comparison or benchmark methods, metrics, graphical checks, decision rules, and reviewer before examining validation results. This reduces after-the-fact selection of only favorable evidence. Formal preregistration is not required for every project.
Criteria should be linked to intended use, scientifically interpretable, justified, and stated before viewing the outcome when practical. They are one part of the evidence, not a substitute for judgment. Do not prescribe universal thresholds.

title: Validation Plan
text:
Proportional planning

Small exploratory analysis
A short validation section in the analysis document may contain the intended claim, a few relevant checks, findings, limitations, and conclusion.


Publication-oriented or collaborative analysis
Identify candidate results, validation questions, diagnostics, sensitivity work, predictive evaluation where applicable, review responsibility, and the decision record.


Operational or high-consequence analysis
Identify decision consequences, independent review where proportionate, explicit performance and limitation criteria, external or prospective evidence where feasible, failure and escalation conditions, and conditions requiring retraining, refitting, or reevaluation.

title: Validation Plan
text:
Reviewer independence
Independent review can reduce confirmation bias but is not universally required. Greater independence is more important when the result is operationally consequential, the analyst made many discretionary choices, the model will be reused, it affects public, animal, environmental, or economic decisions, or findings are mixed.

title: Validation Plan
text:
Stop and resolve
Pause validation when candidate results cannot be identified, intended use is unclear, the analysis version changed after readiness was recorded, required validation data were used during model development without disclosure, metrics were selected only after favorable results were seen, important failures are missing, or the claim is broader than the evidence.

title: Sensitivity, Robustness, and Uncertainty
text:
Sensitivity analysis examines how results change when reasonable inputs, assumptions, parameters, or analytical choices change.
Robustness describes whether the main conclusion remains materially similar across those alternatives.
Uncertainty quantification describes how uncertain inputs, parameters, observations, or processes affect estimates and predictions.
Uncertainty propagation carries uncertainty from inputs or parameters into final outputs.

These ideas are related but not interchangeable.

title: Sensitivity, Robustness, and Uncertainty
text:
Important uncertainty sources
Consider measurement error, sampling error, missing data, underreporting, detection probability, spatial-location uncertainty, temporal uncertainty, parameter uncertainty, model-form uncertainty, prior assumptions, scenario uncertainty, initial conditions, environmental inputs, host distributions, future covariates, stochastic variation, and data revisions.

title: Sensitivity, Robustness, and Uncertainty
text:
Consequential analytical choices
Sensitivity work may examine exclusion rules, missing-data approaches, prior distributions, covariate sets, spatial support, temporal aggregation, neighborhood definitions, classification thresholds, parameter ranges, initial conditions, forecast windows, model structures, and baseline assumptions. Focus on choices that could change the scientific or operational conclusion; exhaustive variation of every minor setting is not required.

title: Sensitivity, Robustness, and Uncertainty
text:
Connect uncertainty to conclusions
Record whether uncertainty changes direction of effect, ranking, classification, threshold crossing, estimated geographic extent, forecast warning, intervention recommendation, confidence in a conclusion, or operational decision. Quantified uncertainty is most useful when the record shows whether it changes interpretation, comparison, or action.

title: Sensitivity, Robustness, and Uncertainty
text:
Mixed findings and intervals
If a conclusion changes under reasonable alternatives, do not hide it or automatically declare the analysis useless. Identify the choices driving the change, narrow the claim where appropriate, record the result as limited or inconclusive, and return to Analyze if a revised analysis is warranted.
Assess whether intervals are based on stated uncertainty sources, interpreted correctly, compatible with intended use, evaluated for coverage when prediction is involved, and not presented as including omitted sources. Narrow intervals are not automatically strong evidence.

title: Validate
text: Validation is not one test and not a final stamp of truth. It is a structured assessment of whether available evidence supports candidate results for a defined use, population, place, time, scale, and decision context.

title: Validate
text:
Three questions

Was the recorded analysis carried out correctly and completely?
Does the method behave adequately for its intended scientific purpose?
How strong and how limited is the evidence supporting the candidate result?

title: Validate
text:
Verification versus validation
Verification asks whether the recorded analysis was implemented and completed as intended. Confirming that all simulation replicates ran or that a forecast used the intended training period is verification.
Validation asks whether evidence supports using the result for its stated purpose. Evaluating whether a simulation represents relevant biological behavior or whether a forecast performs on later observations is validation.
Both matter, but they answer different questions. Validation does not prove that a model is universally correct or permanently valid.

title: Validate
text:
Validate workflow

Confirm the analysis version and candidate result IDs.
State the intended use and claims being assessed.
Define validation questions and planned evidence.
Verify analysis inputs, execution, and outputs.
Examine assumptions, diagnostics, and model behavior.
Evaluate predictions or forecasts where applicable.
Examine sensitivity, robustness, and uncertainty.
Compare with independent evidence or expected domain behavior.
Record failed, mixed, and inconclusive findings.
Decide whether candidate results support their stated use.

Conclusion statuses

not yet evaluated
validation in progress

title: Validate
text:
Validation completion gate

Analysis ID and version are identified.
Candidate result IDs are identified.
Intended use and scope are stated.
Validation questions are recorded.
Verification checks are complete or limitations are visible.
Relevant assumptions and diagnostics are reviewed.
Predictive or forecast evaluation is completed where applicable.
Sensitivity and robustness are examined where consequential.
Important uncertainty sources and their effect on interpretation or decisions are described.
Failed, mixed, and inconclusive evidence remains visible.
Evidence locations are linked.
The authoritative validation record is identified.
The overall conclusion uses exactly one allowed conclusion status.
Every substantive conclusion states the use and scope to which it applies.
Decision-maker and decision date are recorded for every completed substantive conclusion.
A superseded record identifies its replacement validation record and, where applicable, replacement analysis.
A responsible analyst or reviewer records the conclusion and date.
The conclusion states the population, geography, time period, scale, horizon, or use to which it applies.
Any required return to Analyze is recorded.

Passing this gate records a scoped conclusion about available evidence. It does not authorize publication, external communication, or operational release.
A scoped validation conclusion may proceed to Collaborate. Inconclusive or not-supported results may still require collaboration to coordinate revision, limitation, discontinuation, or reporting. Validation support does not establish contribution credit or communication readiness.

title: Selection, Retention, and Disposition
text: Preserving everything is neither necessary nor always responsible. Selection should consider scientific significance, support for reported claims, uniqueness, reuse, operational importance, reconstruction cost, applicable obligations, privacy, security, ecological sensitivity, community authority, size, duplication, repository support, environmental cost, and future format or dependency risk.

title: Selection, Retention, and Disposition
text:
Materials commonly considered
As applicable, assess source snapshots, accepted and analysis-ready data, dictionaries, provenance and transformations, code and versions, configuration, environments, seeds and scenarios, execution manifests, QA/QC, results, validation, collaboration and contribution records, communication and release products, corrections, README, handoff, and closeout records.
Do not automatically preserve caches, regenerable temporary files, failed partial downloads, redundant copies, credentials, unapproved protected data, personal scratch files, or intermediate outputs without scientific, operational, or historical value. Record exclusions when they affect understanding or reproducibility.

title: Selection, Retention, and Disposition
text:
Retention authority
Record the source of the retention or disposition requirement: institutional schedule, funder, contract, data-use agreement, repository policy, journal or publisher, ethics or regulation, Indigenous/Tribal/community governance, or a project-specific decision where no higher authority applies. Do not invent a retention period. If the period is unknown, record unresolved, identify the responsible office or role, retain safely, and do not authorize disposal.
For source or received data, retain the authoritative snapshot where permitted, provider identifiers, acquisition dates, checksums, restrictions, and links to corrected or derived versions. Preserve original evidence where possible rather than silently replacing it with normalized data.

title: Selection, Retention, and Disposition
text:
Negative, inconclusive, and unreleased work
Do not discard work solely because a result was negative, validation was inconclusive, a model failed, a manuscript was not submitted, or an operational product was withheld. Preserve when it documents consequential decisions, prevents costly repetition, supports accountability, or is required by authority or agreement.

title: Selection, Retention, and Disposition
text:
Stop and resolve
Stop disposition when a legal or records hold may apply, an investigation or audit is active, an agreement is unclear, community authority is unresolved, the only consequential copy would be lost, transfer is not accepted, or protected data would move to an unauthorized location. Nonselection records what was assessed, why it was not selected, who decided, which authority applied, where it remains temporarily, and expected later action. Nonselection is not destruction authorization.

title: Preservation Packages, Manifests, and Metadata
text:
A package should have a package ID, project ID, title, version, creation date, responsible owner, authoritative location, selection record, manifest, relationships, restrictions, and access conditions. Here, an artifact means a retained file, dataset, record, code version, or other project material. Include proportionately a README, manifest, checksums, data and metadata, code, configuration, environment records, analysis/validation, communication/release records, licenses, agreements, citations, limitations, exclusions, and deposit instructions. Never include credentials, tokens, passwords, private keys, or encryption keys.
For each artifact, use exactly: planned for inclusion, included, externally referenced, excluded with rationale, unavailable, or superseded. The safe default is planned for inclusion. Included means contained; externally referenced means retained elsewhere under an identifiable durable reference; excluded means deliberately omitted with explanation; unavailable means expected but unobtainable with a limitation; superseded means replaced by an identified artifact/version. Do not rely on temporary personal locations as external preservation references.
An included local file needs a relative package path. An external reference needs a durable identifier and location. An exclusion needs rationale. An unavailable item needs a limitation. A superseded item needs a replacement. A verified local file needs checksum evidence where proportionate. Restricted artifacts identify the restriction without exposing protected content.
For the package manifest, use exactly these verification statuses: not verified, verified, verified with limitation, failed, and not applicable. The safe default is not verified. Not verified means no completed check is recorded. Verified means identity, expected package relationship, and integrity evidence were checked as applicable; an included local file needs relative path, size, format/media type, checksum algorithm, checksum, checksum date, and result where proportionate. Repository-generated integrity evidence is acceptable when the repository is authoritative and recorded. Verified with limitation records the limitation in inclusion_or_exclusion_rationale or notes and links it to the preservation record when consequential. Failed records failure, responsible person/process, next action, and whether a recovery source exists in notes. Not applicable is only for a genuine case with no independently verifiable file content, not merely because verification was not performed.

title: Preservation Packages, Manifests, and Metadata
text:
Packaging approaches
The project may use an ordinary documented directory, repository-specific deposit package, BagIt, RO-Crate, or another accepted institutional/domain format. No packaging standard is universal. BagIt RFC 8493 can support transfer and checksum manifests; RO-Crate can describe relationships among research artifacts; PREMIS concepts can help describe preservation objects, events, rights, and agents. None is required here.
ZIP, TAR, or another archive may be used for transfer, but the record should also identify contents, format, compression, checksum, extraction test, size, and relevant software. Do not rely on an opaque archive with no external manifest or guide.

title: Preservation Packages, Manifests, and Metadata
text:
Dynamic sources and metadata
For APIs, databases, dashboards, websites, or changing services, record snapshot date, query and parameters, source version, schema, response/export format, current-through date, workflow, service documentation, and whether the same response can be recreated. Metadata should identify object, version, responsible agent, dates, format, size, checksums, rights, relationships, preservation actions, repository, identifiers, access conditions, and dependencies. It may live in the manifest, README, repository record, release record, or linked durable record; avoid unnecessary duplication.

title: Formats, Software, Environments, and Reuse
text: Record format, version, media type, encoding, creating/reading software, compression, encryption, and format limitations. Prefer documented, widely supported, non-lossy formats where reasonable, but do not convert merely to appear archival.

title: Formats, Software, Environments, and Reuse
text:
Original and migrated versions
When normalization or migration occurs, retain the original where permitted, identify the migrated copy, tool/version, date, reason, validation, information or behavior lost, and relationship between versions. A migrated file must not silently replace the original. Record the characteristics that must remain intact for meaning or function, such as coordinates and CRS, raster alignment, table values and types, image resolution, sequence identifiers, software behavior, workflow order, timestamps, time zones, and interactive functionality.
Record a meaningful migration or recovery as a preservation event with a source, resulting object/package, reason, tool/process and version, responsible person, date, validation, information lost or changed, earlier-version availability, replacement identifier, and event status. A failed fixity check and recovery is an event even when the recovered package appears unchanged.

title: Formats, Software, Environments, and Reuse
text:
Software and dependencies
Preserve proportionately source, commit/release, license, README, dependencies, lockfiles, build instructions, tests, configuration, example inputs/expected outputs, containers, environment files, interpreter/compiler versions, external tools, HPC modules, database versions, and service requirements. A container does not guarantee indefinite execution. Do not copy proprietary software without authorization.
Distinguish source preserved, workflow documented, environment reconstructable, rerun successful, outputs reproduced, partial reproduction, and interpretation possible but execution unavailable. For large simulations or HPC work, preserve inputs, code, parameters, seeds, representative/principal outputs, summaries, diagnostics, logs, and regeneration instructions where proportionate; record omitted regenerable outputs and future limitations.
The Software Heritage documentation can help archive and reference public source code, but it is not required and may not be suitable for restricted or proprietary code.

title: Access, Governance, Maintenance, and Deaccession
text:
Preservation does not mean openness. Preserved content may be public, internal, controlled, restricted, confidential, embargoed, or governed by an agreement or Indigenous, Tribal, or community authority. Record classification, authority, permitted users/uses, request route, restrictions, review or expiry, and responsible contact. Public availability does not grant unrestricted reuse.
Do not silently broaden access as time passes. Review agreement expiration, partner or community direction, privacy/security classification, repository terms, embargo, license, authorization, and custodian changes. FAIR-oriented practice does not require unrestricted access.

title: Access, Governance, Maintenance, and Deaccession
text:
Maintenance ownership
Identify preservation owner, backup owner, repository account owner, access-review owner, technical contact, funding/fee owner, and next review date or trigger. Avoid a personal account as the only control point. Review repository availability, identifier resolution, access, retrieval, checksums, format risk, dependencies, fees, service ownership, legal/agreement changes, and pending migrations proportionately.

title: Access, Governance, Maintenance, and Deaccession
text:
Migration and repository closure
Record original and new package/artifact, reason, tool/process and version, responsible person, date, checks, information lost/changed, replacement identifier, event type/status, and whether the earlier version remains available. Use the preservation-plan migration-event record for format migration, package migration, repository transfer, metadata correction, access-condition change, fixity failure and recovery, or other events. Migration does not automatically supersede the earlier record. When a repository, project, service, or organization ends, identify successor ownership, export and verify transfer where authorized, update identifiers/contacts, preserve old-to-new relationships, notify affected users/partners, and retain closeout records.

title: Access, Governance, Maintenance, and Deaccession
text:
Deaccession and supersession
Deaccession means an authorized decision to remove a preserved object or package from active repository custody or access. Before deaccession, record prior deposit evidence, original location and identifier, package/version, deaccession authority, governing policy/agreement/process, legal-hold and retention reviews, partner/community review, reason/date, affected users/partners/communities, notification, retained metadata or tombstone, final disposition/replacement, and responsible owner. Record a durable decision; it does not by itself authorize physical destruction, and no deletion procedure belongs here. Superseded and deaccessioned records remain historically identifiable, and replacement packages do not automatically inherit verification or access decisions.

title: Plan a Project
text: Planning records the conditions that make later work understandable and finishable. It does not require a separate planning document: a README, charter, project notes, or another durable artifact may hold the information.

Bound the project.

title: Plan a Project
text:
Is a separate charter warranted?






Conditionally required



A standalone charter is warranted when the project has multiple contributors or organizations, publication intent, external funding or formal deliverables, operational use, sensitive or governed data, substantial computational expense, long duration, formal handoff expectations, or consequential policy, regulatory, or management use. A small exploratory project may keep purpose, owner, scope, outputs, and status in its README.


The decision itself should be visible. Record “README scope is sufficient” or link the charter; do not create a formal file only to satisfy a checklist.

title: Plan a Project
text:
Initiation gate

Objective, intended output, owner, authoritative location, and status are recorded.
Included and excluded work, dependencies, and assumptions are visible.
Roles and decision authority are assigned.
Project consequence and complexity are classified proportionately.
Anticipated data, restrictions, storage, computing, and external dependencies are identified.
Completion criteria and review authority are stated.
A README or charter contains the required scope information.
Unresolved institutional questions are linked to Open Policy Decisions.

This gate authorizes planning to proceed to data-management planning and acquisition; it does not approve analysis or release.

title: Plan a Project
text:
Evidence and interpretation
The planning workflow draws on the existing resource catalog, especially The Turing Way, Good Enough Practices in Scientific Computing, RDMkit, DataONE, and the TIER Protocol. These sources support explicit project purpose, durable documentation, version control, data-management planning, reproducibility, and handoff. Access date: 2026-08-05. External guidance informs this workflow but does not establish GeoEpi or institutional policy.

Sensitive spatial information
Do not prescribe one masking method. Record sensitivity, access restriction, generalization or masking, difference between protected and released representations, and authorization for downstream use. Link unresolved questions to Open Policy Decisions.

title: Spatial and Temporal Conventions
text:
Temporal meaning
Distinguish event, onset, collection, report, extraction, acquisition, processing, model/simulation, publication, and release dates. Record time zone, UTC conversion, daylight-saving behavior, local versus universal timestamps, ambiguous/nonexistent local times, and precision.

title: Spatial and Temporal Conventions
text:
Periods and intervals
Document start/end boundaries, inclusive/exclusive rules, observation interval, aggregation period, partial periods, incomplete weeks/months, rolling windows, and temporal support versus timestamp.
For epidemiological weeks, record week system, week-year convention, start day, week 53 treatment, conversion code, and relationship to source dates. Do not use “week 1” without naming the week-year convention.

title: Spatial and Temporal Conventions
text:
Recurring snapshots and revisions
Record extraction timestamp, reporting delay, late-arriving records, historical revisions, changed case definitions, changed boundaries, backfill behavior, and freeze/cutoff dates.

title: Spatial and Temporal Conventions
text:
Spatiotemporal identifiers
When useful, a stable identifier may combine spatial unit, temporal unit, scenario, layer, and source snapshot. Do not rely on row order as a spatiotemporal identifier.

title: Spatial and Temporal Conventions
text:
Structural checks

Expected CRS, datum, extent, resolution, and alignment are recorded where applicable.
Geometry validity, NoData, masks, and boundary versions are documented.
Expected date range and complete or documented temporal sequence are recorded.
Week-year combinations and time zones are valid.
No unintended duplicate space-time keys exist.
No unexplained coordinate or date loss occurred.

title: Project and Data Structure
text: Structure should allow a reviewer or future collaborator to determine which objects were received, transformed, authoritative, temporary, regenerable, or used to support a reported result.

title: Project and Data Structure
text:
Define object roles







Role
Meaning and minimum control




Preserved source
Original received representation, retained without undocumented editing, linked to source and snapshot IDs, and subject to access restrictions.


Staged
Controlled representation produced from the preserved source; suitable for normalization, linkage, and structural QA, but not necessarily analysis-ready.


Derived
Dataset created through documented transformation, such as aggregates, features, standardized layers, or linked data.


Analysis-ready
Staged or derived data that passed the Organize gate; this status is not scientific validation.


Configuration
Paths, parameters, conventions, source IDs, and transformation settings.


Documentation
README, data dictionary, dataset record, transformation ledger, decisions, limitations, and QA results.


Outputs
Consequential products produced by analysis or reporting; not interchangeable with staged or derived data.


Logs
Execution, warnings, failures, retries, checks, and manual interventions.


Cache or temporary
Removable or regenerable objects whose role is documented and which are not the only copy of a consequential object.

title: Project and Data Structure
text:
No universal folder tree
The Lab Book does not prescribe one universal directory tree. Every project must document the role of each major location, which location is authoritative, which objects are tracked in Git, which are stored externally, which are generated, which are temporary, and how protected data are separated.

title: Project and Data Structure
text:
Repository versus data storage
Git is appropriate for code, configuration, documentation, and small nonrestricted fixtures. It is generally inappropriate for credentials, protected data, large source datasets, sensitive coordinates, caches, and nonredistributable files. Repository paths may point to approved external authoritative locations. Absolute personal paths must not be the only method of locating data.

title: Project and Data Structure
text:
Generated versus maintained objects
Identify whether each major object is manually maintained, received externally, generated deterministically, generated stochastically, cached, archived, or superseded. Generated artifacts should identify producing code and inputs.

title: Project and Data Structure
text:
Common failure modes

A “final” CSV is edited manually after the script ran.
Source and cleaned data are mixed in one directory.
Multiple unversioned files are named final.
A report depends on an undocumented object in a user workspace.
Temporary HPC output is treated as an authoritative result.
Staged data cannot be tied to a source snapshot.

title: Project and Data Structure
text:
Structure checklist

Major locations and object roles are documented.
Preserved source, staged, derived, temporary, configuration, documentation, logs, and outputs are distinguishable.
Authoritative locations and external storage boundaries are recorded.
Protected data and credentials are separated from Git-tracked material.
Generated objects identify their inputs and producing code.
Temporary objects are not the only copy of consequential data.

title: Identifiers and Schema

title: Identifiers and Schema
text:
Record identifiers
Document natural, surrogate, composite, repeated-observation, hierarchical, spatial-unit, temporal, sample, sequence, facility, herd, animal, case, and observation identifiers as applicable. Do not construct identifiers from sensitive fields unless authorized.
For each important key, state whether it is unique, unique within a group, repeatable across time, nonmissing, stable across snapshots, supplied by the source or generated locally, and safe to disclose.

title: Identifiers and Schema
text:
Duplicates and relationships
Distinguish byte-for-byte duplicate files, duplicate rows, legitimate repeated observations, duplicate identifiers, conflicting records, revised records, and multiple reports of one event. Identical values are not automatically duplicate observations.
Document primary keys, foreign keys, relationship cardinality, expected match rate, unmatched records, many-to-many joins, deduplication before joining, aggregation order, and snapshot/temporal compatibility.






Stop and resolve



An accidental many-to-many join can multiply records while producing plausible-looking outputs. Stop when join losses, unexpected multiplication, or conflicting keys cannot be explained.

title: Identifiers and Schema
text:
Schema definition
Build on the existing data dictionary template. A usable schema documents field name, description, type, unit, allowed values/codes, missing-value convention, identifier role, date/time convention, spatial meaning, temporal support, derivation, quality notes, and schema version where warranted.

title: Identifiers and Schema
text:
Types and parsing
Review automatic type guessing for consequential datasets. Check strings with leading zeroes, categorical codes, locale-dependent numbers, dates, Boolean values, censored values, scientific notation, large integers, coordinate precision, and encoding.

title: Identifiers and Schema
text:
Units and missingness
Record unit definition, scale, denominator where relevant, original and standardized units, conversion rule, and mixed-unit handling. Distinguish not observed, not applicable, suppressed, below detection, not reported, withheld, structurally absent, parsing failure, and true zero. Do not collapse these states without recording the consequence.

title: Identifiers and Schema
text:
Categorical codes and schema versions
For each code, record code, label, definition, source/version, valid period when codes change, and handling of unknown or deprecated values. Create a new schema version when fields, types, units, code meanings, identifier meanings, temporal support, or spatial support affect interpretation or compatibility.

title: Identifiers and Schema
text:
Domain examples

Surveillance records: case ID, case-definition version, facility/jurisdiction key, event/report dates, and revision status.
Field observations: observation ID, taxon ID, site key, effort, unit, and detection-limit convention.
Sequence metadata: sample ID, accession, host/location restriction, collection date, and reference version.
Spatial polygons: stable area ID, boundary version, CRS, geometry status, and spatial support.
Weekly rasters: tile/layer ID, week-year, CRS, origin/alignment, NoData, and mask.
Simulation inputs: scenario ID, parameter-set version, units, and initial/boundary conditions.

title: Review, Approval, Release, and Corrections
text: Review examines a defined product version for a defined purpose. Approval is a decision by the applicable authority. Release is the event that makes one exact product version available to an identified audience through an identified channel. Peer review, collaboration readiness, release approval, and release are distinct.

title: Review, Approval, Release, and Corrections
text:
Ready for release review
The communication-product record is authoritative. Use exactly not ready for release review, ready for release review, or ready for release review with documented limitation; default to not ready for release review. A ready status requires the exact product and package, audience, purpose, channel, result and validation IDs, collaboration record, claim traceability, uncertainty, limitations, availability, restrictions, reviews, and release authority. A limitation status also requires a substantive limitation, why it matters, affected scope, downstream caution, follow-up, and responsible follow-up. Decision-maker and ISO 8601 date remain blank while not ready.

title: Review, Approval, Release, and Corrections
text:
Release decision and event
Default the release decision to not yet reviewed for specified release. Use exactly not yet reviewed for specified release, approved for specified release, approved for specified release with documented condition, not approved for specified release, deferred for specified release, or superseded before release decision. The proposed package must be identified before any substantive decision; approval applies only to one product ID and version, package, audience, channel, purpose, and recorded restrictions and availability conditions. The exact approved package must match the proposed package unless the authority explicitly requires a revised package.
An approved condition requires the condition, why it matters, affected audience, purpose, channel, claim, or use, required warning or limitation, follow-up, responsible follow-up, and expiration or reconsideration date where relevant. Empty or none condition fields are not allowed. Not approved requires rationale, blocking concern, authority, decision date, required return stage or terminal disposition, and corrective owner; it is not withdrawal or withholding and does not imply that the underlying result is invalid. Deferred requires reason, unresolved dependency, responsible person, and reconsideration condition or date; it is not approval or nonapproval and does not permit release. Superseded before decision requires replacement product ID/version, reason, date, and responsible owner; the replacement does not inherit readiness, review, or approval.
Default the release state to not released. Use exactly not released, released, withheld, withdrawn, or superseded. Not released means no distribution or publication event occurred and may coexist with any release-decision status. Released requires an approved decision, exact version, release date, location or distribution record, audience, channel, purpose, applicable condition or warning, and persistent identifier where one exists. Withheld is an affirmative decision not to distribute a prepared product and requires authority, reason, date, affected audience or channel, reconsideration or terminal disposition, and notification where applicable; it is not a synonym for not released. Withholding may follow approval only when the authority deliberately stops distribution and records why. Withdrawn requires a previous release, original release record, authority, reason, date, affected claims or uses, notification, replacement or next action, and whether underlying results remain supported. Superseded requires replacement product ID/version, replacement release-record ID where applicable, reason, date, and responsible owner.
Released cannot accompany a nonapproved decision. Withdrawn requires earlier release evidence. Superseded requires a replacement. Not released must not contain a release date or released location. An embargoed product is not released to the embargoed audience until the release event occurs. Approval alone does not change release state to released.

title: Review, Approval, Release, and Corrections
text:
Corrections, withdrawals, and supersession
Keep the earlier product identifiable. Use exactly one correction category: typographical or formatting; no change to meaning, factual correction; no change to scientific conclusion, corrected figure or table, corrected availability, citation, or attribution statement, corrected data release, corrected code or software release, scientific correction affecting interpretation, withdrawal, publisher- or authority-defined retraction, or other. A typographical correction may remain in Communicate. A corrected figure or table remains in Communicate only when underlying scientific results do not change. A changed result returns to Analyze; changed scientific support or interpretation returns to Validate; contributor or attribution changes may require Collaborate. Use retraction only when the applicable publisher or authority formally uses it.
For consequential corrections, retain the original product and release record, type, description, reason, affected claims, whether conclusions changed, authority, date, notification, corrected or replacement version, and return-to-lifecycle-stage decision. Do not silently overwrite the scientific history. For significant scholarly updates, consult applicable publisher or registry practice such as Crossref versioning and corrections guidance.
Withdrawal records why access stopped, who decided, what audience was notified, and what remains identifiable. A superseded product and superseded release point to their replacements, reason, date, and responsible owner; replacement records do not inherit claim acceptance, readiness, approval, accessibility review, availability statements, or release state automatically. Link final release, correction, withdrawal, and supersession records to Preserve: the released package and preservation package may differ, the preservation record identifies what was selected, withdrawal does not automatically require destruction of preserved history, superseded releases should link to preserved replacements, and access restrictions continue into Preserve. Long-term preservation and retention decisions are authoritative in Preserve and applicable policy/agreement.

title: Communicate
text:
Communicate begins when a project or defined result package is ready for communication or ready for communication with documented limitation. It prepares a defined product for a defined audience; it does not make new scientific evidence.
Communication may change form and level of detail, but it must not silently broaden, strengthen, or alter the evidence. A product represents selected results, claims, audience, purpose, version, limitations, and access conditions. Even an internal product may influence operations, policy, funding, partners, or later publications.

title: Communicate
text:
Communicate workflow

Identify the project or result package approved to enter Communicate.
Define the audience, purpose, intended action, product, and channel.
Identify exact result and validation records.
Draft claims within validated scope and record consequential claim-to-evidence links.
Include uncertainty and limitations where they affect interpretation or action.
Prepare figures, tables, maps, captions, and accessible alternatives.
Apply relevant reporting guidance proportionately.
Prepare accurate data, code, software, contribution, funding, restriction, and availability statements.
Review the exact product version and record responses.
Decide whether it is ready for release review.
Record the authorized release decision.
Release, withhold, withdraw, or supersede the exact version; transfer selected history to Preserve.

title: Communicate
text:
Product-preparation status
Use exactly: planned, in preparation, under review, revision required, ready for release review, or superseded. The safe default is planned. These statuses describe preparation, not release approval.

title: Communicate
text:
Ready-for-release-review status
Use exactly: not ready for release review, ready for release review, or ready for release review with documented limitation. The safe default is not ready for release review. The product record is authoritative. A ready status means the exact product is sufficiently complete for the applicable authority to consider; it does not approve or release the product. A limitation status requires a nonempty limitation, why it matters, affected scope, downstream caution, follow-up, and responsible follow-up.
These are two separate status systems. Product-preparation status describes where work on the product stands. Release-review readiness records the authoritative decision that one exact product package is complete enough for release authority to consider. planned, in preparation, under review, and revision required require readiness to remain not ready for release review. Product-preparation status may become ready for release review only when readiness is either ready for release review or ready for release review with documented limitation. A superseded product must not retain a ready status and must identify its replacement communication-product ID and version.
Changing a product after a ready decision requires a new product version and a renewed readiness decision. Minor formatting changes may retain the same version only when the project’s versioning convention permits it and scientific meaning is unchanged.
Every superseded product records its replacement ID, replacement version, reason, date, and responsible owner. Acceptance, readiness, approval, accessibility review, availability statements, and release state do not transfer automatically; repeat affected checks for the replacement.

title: Communicate
text:
Boundary and return paths
Communicate does not replace Analyze, Validate, Collaborate, legal review, privacy authorization, institutional clearance, or preservation. Released products may proceed to Preserve, while withheld or unreleased products may also be selected for preservation. Correction and supersession records remain part of preserved history; release does not establish deposit or preservation verification. If communication reveals changed data, methods, parameters, estimates, or outputs, return to Analyze. If it reveals changed scientific support, interpretation, performance evidence, or limitations, return to Validate. If it changes contributors, credit, partner obligations, or decision authority, return to Collaborate. Do not silently correct scientific content only in the product.

title: Data, Code, Software, and Availability
text:
Availability statements must describe actual access. State whether data, code, software, parameters, environments, and supplementary products are open, controlled, restricted, embargoed, unavailable, or available on request, and identify the responsible contact or access route where appropriate. Public availability is not permission to reuse; restricted data should not be made public merely for reproducibility.
Record exact versions, repositories or locations, persistent identifiers where available, licenses without interpreting them, dependencies, and any missing inputs that limit reproduction. Cite data as identifiable products when appropriate using DataCite data-citation guidance, and cite software versions using the FORCE11 Software Citation Principles. A DOI is not required for every output.
Include partner, Indigenous, Tribal, community, confidentiality, privacy, security, and contractual conditions. Use “available on request” only when an actual request process exists, a responsible office, role, or contact is identified, the project has authority to provide access, eligibility and restrictions are stated, the materials can realistically be located and transferred, and expected duration of access or maintenance is known where relevant. Prefer precise wording such as publicly available at an identified version, available through controlled access, available under a named agreement or review process, available only in aggregated or synthetic form, or not shareable under the recorded restriction. If unavailable inputs prevent exact reproduction, state what can and cannot be reproduced.
Availability statements are part of Communicate, not authorization for access or a substitute for legal, privacy, partner, or governance decisions. Changes to access authority return to Collaborate.

title: Audience, Purpose, and Products
text:
Begin with intended use. Record the audience, what it needs to understand, intended action or decision, product type, channel, internal or external status, urgency, expected lifespan, consequence of misunderstanding, and restrictions on who may receive it.
The same validated result may support different products, but each product needs its own audience, claims, scope, and review. Possible products include manuscripts, technical reports, internal memos, briefs, presentations, posters, maps, dashboards, forecast bulletins, surveillance summaries, data or software releases, model documentation, public summaries, and training material. No universal product is required.

title: Audience, Purpose, and Products
text:
Product identity
For a consequential product, record a stable product ID, title, version, owner, authoritative location, status, audience, result IDs, validation-record IDs, collaboration record, and expected release route. An internal product is not automatically unreviewed or unrestricted; it may influence management, operations, policy, field activity, funding, partners, or later publications.

title: Audience, Purpose, and Products
text:
Time-sensitive products
For forecasts, dashboards, bulletins, and operational summaries, record data current through, forecast origin, forecast horizon, issue time, next update, expiration or stale-after condition, superseding product, and responsible owner. A live URL does not make an old product current.

title: Audience, Purpose, and Products
text:
Plain language
Use plain language when it helps the audience. Lead with the main message, define necessary technical terms, identify the action, and retain qualifications. Do not simplify by removing the population, period, geography, denominator, uncertainty, or limitation that gives a result meaning.

title: Audience, Purpose, and Products
text:
Stop and resolve
Pause when audience or purpose is unclear; the product exceeds validated scope; release authority is unknown; access or partner conditions are unresolved; a product is called current without a valid date; the intended action is unsupported; or protected data or locations would be exposed.

title: Roles, Responsibilities, and Decisions
text:
Possible roles include project lead, data provider, data steward, analytical lead, modeling lead, subject-matter contributor, technical or code reviewer, statistical or methodological reviewer, validation reviewer, operational owner, partner liaison, communication-preparation owner, release authority, repository maintainer, and future maintainer.
One person may hold several roles. Several people may share a role when the division is clear. Do not require every project to use every role.

title: Roles, Responsibilities, and Decisions
text:
Consequential decisions
Examples include changing project scope, replacing a data source, changing an outcome or case definition, changing model structure, selecting a primary result, accepting a validation limitation, sharing restricted data or outputs, changing contributor credit, selecting a version to communicate, changing an operational owner, and approving a handoff.
Routine coding and formatting decisions do not require formal decision ownership.

title: Roles, Responsibilities, and Decisions
text:
Decision records
Use the lightest durable record that preserves the decision, options considered where consequential, rationale, evidence used, responsible person or role, required reviewer, date, affected project/data/analysis/validation/result version, and follow-up. A README history, project note, GitHub issue or pull request, meeting decision summary, existing decision log, or exception record may be sufficient. Do not create a new decision log when an existing durable record is adequate.

title: Roles, Responsibilities, and Decisions
text:
Consensus and disagreement
Consensus may be useful, but it is not universally required. Scientific evidence is not replaced by a vote. Keep disagreement visible when it affects interpretation, risk, access, credit, or communication. The person with authority should record the final decision and rationale; a minority or unresolved scientific concern may remain a limitation.

title: Roles, Responsibilities, and Decisions
text:
Backup responsibility
For long-running, operational, externally funded, high-cost, or high-consequence work, identify a backup contact, current-status location, principal workflow entry point, access owner, and plan for an extended absence. Do not require backup roles for every small exploratory analysis.

title: Collaborate
text: Collaboration is more than adding names to a project or inviting people to meetings. Defensible collaboration makes clear what is being produced, who contributes, who reviews consequential work, who decides, where current records are located, how disagreements are handled, how credit is discussed, and what happens when a contributor joins, leaves, or changes role.

title: Collaborate
text:
Collaboration is cross-cutting
People collaborate during planning, data acquisition, analysis, and validation. This stage collects the practices needed to coordinate shared work; it does not imply that collaboration begins only after validation. The post-Validate checkpoint focuses on coordinating validated results and contributor responsibilities before communication products are prepared.
Collaboration is not consensus, validation, approval, an authorship policy, a legal agreement, or release authorization. Access follows authorization and purpose, not project membership alone.

title: Collaborate
text:
Collaborate workflow

Identify the project, contributors, organizations, and current phase.
State the shared purpose and expected outputs.
Assign roles and decision responsibility.
Identify authoritative locations for data, code, decisions, outputs, and review records.
Agree how changes, reviews, and disagreements will be recorded.
Confirm access and sharing restrictions.
Record contributions and revisit credit expectations.
Coordinate required scientific, technical, operational, or governance review.
Identify unresolved issues and required return to Analyze or Validate.
Confirm continuity, backup responsibility, and handoff needs.
Decide whether coordinated work is ready to enter Communicate.

title: Collaborate
text:
Ready-for-communication statuses
Use exactly:

not ready for communication
ready for communication
ready for communication with documented limitation

The safe default is not ready for communication. The authoritative decision belongs in a collaboration agreement or equivalent project-level collaboration record, not in an individual contributor record, review comment, validation record, or result row.
Not ready for communication is the default while the decision-maker or decision date is blank. It records no readiness decision; unresolved work may remain visible.
Ready for communication requires the current project/result package and versions, validation-record IDs, a communication-preparation owner, required reviews complete, no unresolved concern or an accepted documented exception, recorded restrictions, and a decision-maker plus ISO 8601 decision date.
Ready for communication with documented limitation requires all of the ready fields plus a nonempty limitation, why it matters, affected product, claim, result, audience, use, geography, or period, downstream caution or restriction, follow-up, responsible follow-up, decision-maker, and ISO 8601 decision date. Do not use this status with blank limitation fields.

title: Collaborate
text:
Ready-for-communication gate

Project and result versions are identified.
Relevant validation records and scoped conclusions are identified.
Intended communication products are named at a general level.
Active contributors and organizations are identified.
Responsibilities and consequential decision authority are clear.
Required reviews are complete or their limitations are visible.
Review findings and responses are recorded.
Unresolved disagreements are visible.
Changes requiring return to Analyze or Validate are completed or explicitly deferred with a limitation.
Authoritative locations are identified.
Access, sharing, confidentiality, license, and partner restrictions are recorded.
Contribution and credit expectations have been discussed proportionately.
External partner conditions are recorded where applicable.
A communication-preparation owner is identified.
Continuity or backup responsibility is identified where risk warrants it.
The readiness decision and ISO 8601 date are recorded.
One exact readiness status is used.

Passing this gate means that contributors have coordinated the work well enough to begin preparing communication products. It does not authorize submission, publication, public release, operational use, or unrestricted sharing.
When the status is ready for communication, proceed to Communicate. When it is ready for communication with documented limitation, carry every substantive limitation into the communication-product record. When it is not ready for communication, do not proceed. Collaboration readiness is not release approval.

title: Contributions, Credit, and Authorship
text: Record actual contributions and revisit expected credit as work changes. This record does not itself determine authorship.

title: Contributions, Credit, and Authorship
text:
Contribution records
Record contributor, organization or affiliation, project role, contribution description, related data/code/analysis/validation/result/output IDs, contribution period, expected recognition, optional CRediT role(s), discussion status, contributor confirmation and date, and review date. Keep unresolved credit questions visible.
The contribution and credit template is a reusable starting point. A formal record is not required for every temporary collaborator or small exploratory project.

title: Contributions, Credit, and Authorship
text:
Credit and authorship
Distinguish authorship, named contributor, acknowledgment, data/software/dataset citation, and partner or organization recognition. Substantial data, software, field, validation, visualization, and technical work should remain visible even when the recognition form differs. Requirements vary by discipline, journal, institution, funder, community, contract, and product. Before communication is finalized, confirm names, affiliations, contributions, recognition form, authorship, order, and disputes as applicable. Do not infer authorship or author order from a role title, a single contribution, or the use of the optional CRediT vocabulary.
The NISO CRediT contributor-role resource can describe contribution types, but it does not determine authorship or author order and is voluntary. Applicable institutional, contractual, journal, funder, community, and legal requirements take precedence. The resource is also recorded in the local resource catalog.
Use these discussion statuses exactly: not yet discussed, discussion in progress, agreed, disputed, not applicable, and superseded. “Agreed” requires the expected recognition, contributor confirmation and date, and maintainer review date; if confirmation is unavailable, record the attempt, reason, authority, or exception rather than silently marking agreement. “Disputed” records the contribution or recognition at issue, affected contributors, positions or evidence, guidance, authority, current state, and communication effect. “Not applicable” is only for a genuine non-applicability. “Superseded” links a replacement contribution record or row and records the supersession date, reason, and maintainer.

title: Contributions, Credit, and Authorship
text:
Changes and disputes
Record the date, change or dispute, affected contributors, rationale or positions, decision authority, resolution or unresolved state, and effect on communication readiness. Do not make a copied record appear agreed, confirmed, or approved.

title: Results and Traceability
text:
A result record connects an important reported value, figure, table, map, forecast, simulation summary, or operational product to the data, code, settings, execution, and output that produced it.

A result record connects an important reported value, figure, table, map, forecast, simulation summary, or operational product to the data, code, settings, execution, and output that produced it.
analysis-ready dataset
