title: Results and Traceability
text:
When to create one
A result record is useful when an output is included in a manuscript, shared outside the immediate team, used in an operational decision, used in a presentation or report, compared across scenarios, expensive to regenerate, likely to be revised, or consequential to the project’s conclusion. Not every temporary plot requires a separate record. Closely related outputs may share one record when their inputs, run, status, and interpretation are the same.

title: Results and Traceability
text:
Result identity
Record as appropriate: result ID and name, analysis ID and version, direct input dataset IDs and versions, code version, settings or parameter record, computing environment, run ID, output location, intended use, status, limitations, and a later result that supersedes it. Source lineage remains available through the staged- or derived-dataset record and does not need to be repeated in every result row. A filename alone is not a sufficient result identity. The result traceability template is a compact starting point.

title: Results and Traceability
text:
Result statuses
Use planned, produced, incomplete, candidate for validation, failed, or superseded. The safe default is planned. Produced means the output exists. Candidate for validation means the analysis-level readiness decision selected the result for checking in Validate. Validation itself has not yet occurred.
Keep the levels distinct: a run status describes what happened during one execution; a result status describes what happened to one output; analysis readiness describes whether the documented analysis and its named candidate results may enter Validate. The analysis specification or equivalent analysis-level record is the authoritative readiness decision. Candidate result IDs should be referenced by the validation plan and validation decisions and records.

title: Results and Traceability
text:
Manuscripts and reports
Copying a figure into a manuscript does not preserve its origin. Point the result record to the actual output file, keep captions and table notes consistent with the analysis version, document manually altered figures or tables, and link reported numbers to the same run and result version as the displayed output.

title: Results and Traceability
text:
Superseded results
Do not delete the only record of an earlier result when it influenced a decision, appeared in a draft, was shared externally, was replaced after a correction, or differs because data, code, settings, or scenarios changed. Mark it superseded and identify the replacement.

title: Analyze
text: Analyze is more than obtaining a numerical answer or successfully running code. It connects a scientific or operational question to an analysis-ready dataset, a stated method, recorded settings, a particular execution, generated outputs, and candidate results that can be checked in the Validate stage.

title: Analyze
text:
Analyze boundary
Analyze begins when a staged or derived dataset is recorded as ready for analysis or ready for analysis with documented limitation. The limitation must travel with the analysis record and outputs. Analyze may clarify the objective, define the target, record methods and settings, run scripts or models, preserve warnings and incomplete work, and trace important results.
Analyze does not complete model checking, convergence assessment, residual diagnosis, calibration, predictive-performance assessment, external validation, robustness or sensitivity conclusions, simulation verification, uncertainty adequacy, scientific interpretation, publication approval, or operational approval. Those decisions belong to Validate or later stages.

title: Analyze
text:
Analyze workflow

Confirm the dataset is ready for analysis.
State the analysis question or practical objective.
Define the quantity, contrast, prediction, pattern, or simulation outcome of interest.
Label the work as exploratory, planned, sensitivity, or post hoc.
Record the method, variables, settings, and intended outputs.
Run the analysis from a documented starting point.
Record the execution, including warnings and failures.
Link important results to their data, code, settings, run, and output.
Record changes made after earlier results were viewed.
Decide whether the analysis is ready to enter Validate.






flowchart TD
  data[Analysis-ready dataset] --> question[Question and target]
  question --> method[Method and settings]
  method --> run[Documented execution]
  run --> outputs[Outputs and candidate results]
  outputs --> gate[Ready for validation]






A candidate result is an output that has been produced and recorded but has not passed the future Validate stage. A successful analysis run shows that the recorded procedure produced an output. It does not establish that the method was appropriate, the model fit adequately, the predictions are accurate, or the scientific conclusion is justified.

title: Analyze
text:
Evidence and interpretation
The draft workflow is informed by the existing resource catalog, including The Turing Way, Good Enough Practices in Scientific Computing, the TIER Protocol, FAIR Principles for Research Software, RDMkit, DataONE, and Ecological Forecasting Initiative guidance. These sources support clear objectives, recorded code and settings, reproducible execution, and traceable results. They inform this draft workflow but do not establish GeoEpi or institutional policy. Access date: 2026-08-06.

title: Analyze
text:
Ready-for-validation gate
The safe starting status is not ready for validation. Use only these statuses:

not ready for validation
ready for validation
ready for validation with documented limitation

An analysis may enter future Validate only when:

The question or practical objective is recorded.
The quantity, comparison, prediction, pattern, or simulation outcome is clear.
The dataset ID, version, readiness status, and limitation are recorded.
Exploratory, planned, sensitivity, and post hoc work are labeled appropriately.
Methods, variables, transformations, exclusions, settings, and intended outputs are recorded.
Consequential changes made after viewing results are documented.
Code, settings, software, and computing information can be identified.
Consequential executions have run IDs or a clearly repeatable execution path.
Seeds, scenarios, parameter sets, partitions, and replicates are recorded where applicable.
Expected and produced outputs are compared.
Warnings, failures, retries, cancellations, and incomplete runs are visible.
Important candidate results have traceability records where warranted, and their result IDs are named in the analysis-level readiness decision.
Limitations and unresolved execution problems are visible.
The analysis specification or equivalent analysis-level record is authoritative for readiness.
A responsible analyst or reviewer records the readiness decision and ISO 8601 decision time in that analysis-level record.
Status is explicitly recorded as one of the three statuses above.

Run completion belongs to the run record. Candidate selection belongs to result records and the analysis-level readiness decision. Passing this gate means that the analysis has been specified, executed, and recorded well enough to undergo validation. It does not mean that the analysis has passed validation.

title: Computational Execution
Computational Execution
Computational Execution
text:
Proportional run records
For a simple local analysis, a rendered Quarto document or notebook may be enough when it records the input dataset version, code version, settings, execution date, output, warnings, and limitations. A separate run-record file is not universal.
Use a separate run record when several executions must be compared, settings differ, the work is expensive or consequential, HPC is used, failures and retries matter, responsibility may transfer, or reproducibility depends on external software. The analysis run record template is a reusable starting point.

title: Computational Execution
text:
Execution status
Use planned, running, completed, completed with documented limitation, failed, cancelled, or superseded. Completed means the recorded execution finished and produced its recorded outputs. It does not mean the analysis is valid or ready for validation.

title: Computational Execution
text:
Warnings and partial completion
Compare expected outputs with outputs actually produced. Record warnings, errors, incomplete subsets, failed array tasks, missing scenarios or replicates, cancellations, manual recovery, and retry relationships. A zero exit code or successfully rendered document does not by itself show that every expected result was produced.

title: Computational Execution
text:
Overwrite safety
Do not silently replace an earlier important result. Give revised runs new run IDs, record which run is current, retain failed or superseded records when they affected later decisions, save important outputs under identifiable locations, and do not rely on an unsaved interactive workspace.

title: Computational Execution
text:
Local and HPC execution
The same scientific information should be recoverable whether work ran locally or on a cluster. For HPC, use the existing HPC run record for submission script, job and array IDs, resources, loaded software, inputs, outputs, logs, exit status, retries, and the relationship to local development. This is record-keeping guidance, not an HPC tutorial.

title: Computational Execution
text:
Stop and resolve
Pause readiness when the input version is unknown, code or settings cannot be identified, important output was manually edited, expected outputs are missing without explanation, failed tasks were silently excluded, warnings were discarded, local and cluster software differ materially without documentation, or a result cannot be tied to a specific execution.

title: Recurring and Programmatic Data
text: Recurring acquisition includes APIs, databases, portals, scheduled extracts, surveillance feeds, sensor feeds, automated downloads, and revised historical datasets. Do not implement a client or download script here; record what a reproducible retrieval must preserve.

title: Recurring and Programmatic Data
text:
Record the request specification
Retain the endpoint or database, dataset/table, query, request parameters, date range, geography, variables, filters, pagination behavior, extraction timestamp, API/database version where available, code version, and configuration version. Do not store secrets in configuration committed to Git.

title: Recurring and Programmatic Data
text:
Preserve snapshots
When a retrieval can change, produce a preserved snapshot or immutable release record appropriate to the project. Distinguish the live source, retrieved snapshot, normalized data, and current analytical dataset. A live URL is not a reproducibility identifier.
Each accepted retrieval should produce or update a source inventory record, snapshot or retrieval ID, intake or acceptance status, schema/revision assessment, and a preserved snapshot when the source can change or the workflow consequence warrants it. A retrieval manifest is Conditionally required for multi-file, repeated, transferred, regulated, operational, or integrity-sensitive retrievals.

title: Recurring and Programmatic Data
text:
Revisions and late-arriving data
Document replacement behavior, backfills, corrected records, reporting delays, revised historical periods, schema changes, changed geographic boundaries, and changed case definitions. “Latest” is not an adequate identifier for a reproducible retrieval.

title: Recurring and Programmatic Data
text:
Idempotence and overwrite safety
Recommended: design retrievals that do not silently overwrite prior snapshots, detect existing valid outputs, record partial failure, support safe retry, and distinguish completed, failed, incomplete, and superseded retrievals.






Stronger practice



For a consequential recurring workflow, retain an immutable retrieval manifest and an automated completeness check for every snapshot. This strengthens traceability without making a scheduler, workflow engine, or container universally required.

title: Recurring and Programmatic Data
text:
Pagination and completeness
Before accepting a retrieval, retain evidence that all pages or partitions were retrieved, expected date or spatial coverage is present, rate limiting did not silently truncate results, retries did not duplicate records, and response counts are plausible.
A successful HTTP response, database connection, or completed download command is not evidence of complete retrieval.

title: Recurring and Programmatic Data
text:
Schema drift
Check for added or removed variables, type changes, category changes, renamed fields, changed missing-value conventions, altered units, and changed coordinate definitions. Record how a change was handled; do not silently coerce a new schema into an old one.

title: Recurring and Programmatic Data
text:
Retrieval manifest
Recommended, conditionally required for consequential recurring workflows: retain a manifest containing retrieval ID, source ID, snapshot ID, intake or acceptance status, requested period, request hash where useful, retrieved files, status, timestamps, software/configuration version, checksums where proportionate, log location, schema/revision assessment, and error or retry information.






Example



A weekly environmental raster retrieval should record the requested weeks, geographic tiles, CRS, grid alignment, response status, and snapshot identifier. A recurring surveillance extract should also record the query, case-definition version, report-date window, late-report behavior, and database snapshot or extraction timestamp.

title: Recurring and Programmatic Data
text:
Acceptance gate for recurring data

Request specification and source identifier are versioned.
Retrieval timestamp, requested period, geography, and configuration are recorded.
A snapshot or immutable release record exists when the source can change.
Pagination, partition, coverage, and response-count checks are recorded.
Schema drift and revision behavior are assessed.
Retry, failure, duplicate, incomplete, and superseded states are distinguishable.
Credentials are kept outside committed code, configuration, logs, and templates.
The resulting snapshot is registered through the data-source inventory and, when useful, the file manifest.
The retrieval has an intake or acceptance status, schema/revision assessment, and preserved snapshot when required.

title: Data Intake and Acceptance
text:
Proposed minimum requirement



The Minimum GeoEpi Project Standard requires source protection, provenance, restrictions, metadata, and traceability. Preserve the received source package and record enough evidence to identify, inspect, restrict, and accept or reject it for staging. Intake acceptance does not establish analytical validity, model suitability, publication readiness, or authorization for every downstream use.

title: Data Intake and Acceptance
text:
Definitions for intake

Source: the provider’s conceptual dataset or data system.
Snapshot: a specific received, downloaded, extracted, or released representation of the source.
Intake event: the documented act of receiving or extracting a snapshot.
Preserved source package: the retained original delivered representation before local correction or normalization.
Staged data: a controlled working representation prepared from the preserved source package.
Derived data: data created through documented transformation.
Authoritative location: the location designated as current for a specified artifact; it is not necessarily the provider’s original system.

title: Data Intake and Acceptance
text:
Before receipt
Record or confirm the provider, data owner, access authorization, expected dataset, expected files or tables, format, delivery method, version or time period, geographic and temporal support, restrictions, identifiers, expected documentation, and contact for discrepancies.
Do not accept credentials in README files, Git, templates, or logs.

title: Data Intake and Acceptance
text:
Receive into an approved location
Place incoming data first in an approved source or intake location. The location should prevent accidental overwrite, preserve original names where useful, preserve the delivered package, limit access appropriately, and separate received material from transformed data. No universal folder name or storage platform is required.

title: Data Intake and Acceptance
text:
Assign identifiers
Every received dataset must have project identity or authoritative project context, a source ID, and a snapshot, release, extraction, or acquisition ID sufficient to distinguish the received version. A separate intake ID is Conditionally required when more than one delivery or extraction may occur, replacement or corrected deliveries are possible, multiple people or systems handle intake, a formal manifest or audit trail is needed, or the workflow is recurring, regulated, operational, or high consequence. For a simple one-time delivery, the snapshot or acquisition ID may also serve as the intake ID.

title: Data Intake and Acceptance
text:
Preserve the source package
Retain the original delivered representation where lawful and practical: a downloaded archive, spreadsheet, database extract, API response, sequence files, field-data export, and associated documentation. Do not silently edit the preserved source copy. Corrections and normalization belong in staged or derived representations.

title: Data Intake and Acceptance
text:
Record provenance
At minimum, record source, provider or collector, acquisition method, acquisition date/time where relevant, source identifier, version or release, original filename or table, local authoritative location, restriction or license, access contact, related agreement or documentation, transformation-record location, and a checksum when proportionate. Use the existing data-source inventory rather than creating redundant records.

title: Data Intake and Acceptance
text:
File or object manifest
Use a file-level manifest for a multi-file delivery, archive, repeated snapshot, sequence batch, raster stack, model-input bundle, transfer across systems, or regulated/high-consequence workflow. A checksum is Conditionally required when integrity across transfers, storage systems, releases, or repeated processing materially matters. It is not required for every trivial temporary file.
Use the data-file manifest template.
In that manifest, relative_path is relative to the documented intake or preserved-source root. source_modified_time is the provider’s or source system’s time, not local receipt time, and should include a time zone or an explicit source convention. Checksum fields may be blank when integrity checking is not proportionate. supersedes should reference a stable file, snapshot, or manifest ID. Use the documented intake statuses in validation_status: received, pending validation, pending clarification, accepted for staging, accepted with documented limitation, rejected, or superseded; the row marked as an example must be deleted before use.

title: Data Intake and Acceptance
Data Intake and Acceptance
text:
Initial content inspection
Check only enough to decide whether the delivery is plausible and ready for further organization: identifiers, key variables, units, missing-value conventions, interpretable dates and geography, expected categories, consistent confidentiality markings, and absence of obvious truncation or corruption. Intake inspection is not final analytical QA/QC.

title: Data Intake and Acceptance
text:
Resolve discrepancies
Record the discrepancy, date identified, source contacted, clarification received, replacement delivery, affected files, and acceptance decision. Never silently substitute or overwrite a corrected delivery. Link related deliveries through snapshot or intake identifiers.

title: Data Intake and Acceptance
text:
Status-transition model





flowchart TD
  received[received] --> pending_validation[pending validation]
  pending_validation --> pending_clarification[pending clarification, when needed]
  pending_validation --> accepted_staging[accepted for staging]
  pending_clarification --> accepted_staging
  pending_validation --> rejected[rejected]
  pending_clarification --> rejected
  accepted_staging --> limited[accepted with documented limitation]
  accepted_staging --> superseded[superseded later]
  limited --> superseded






superseded does not delete or overwrite the earlier intake record. Rejection does not necessarily mean that the source is scientifically invalid; it means that this delivery must not enter staging. A pending delivery must not silently enter downstream analysis. An accepted-with-limitation decision must record the limitation, likely consequence, downstream restriction, responsible decision-maker, and required follow-up.

title: Data Intake and Acceptance
text:
Acceptance statuses
Use only these statuses for this intake workflow: received means material has arrived but has not been inspected; pending validation means technical or content inspection is incomplete; pending clarification means a material question has been sent to the provider or owner; accepted for staging means the delivery may enter the Organize stage; accepted with documented limitation means it may enter staging with a visible limitation and responsible decision-maker; rejected means it must not enter staging; and superseded means a later identified delivery replaces it while the original record remains preserved. These labels guide the workflow and do not establish institutional classification terminology.






Stop and resolve



Pause intake or analysis when authorization is missing or unclear; unexpected PII or protected information is present; restrictions conflict with the planned workflow; the source or version cannot be identified; required files are absent; corruption is suspected; identifiers cannot be reconciled; temporal fields are ambiguous; CRS or spatial support cannot be determined; the delivery differs materially from its description; replacement files overwrite prior evidence; or the intended storage location is not approved.
These conditions require clarification, not improvised assumptions.

title: Data Intake and Acceptance
text:
Domain-specific intake checks

Spatial data
Record CRS, datum, units, extent, resolution, grid origin/alignment, masks, boundary version, and NoData convention.


Epidemiological and surveillance data
Record case-definition version, event/report/extract dates, denominator, deduplication, jurisdiction, reporting delay, and confidentiality.


Ecological and field data
Record sampling effort, collector, instrument, calibration, taxonomic identifiers, detection limits, and field revisions.


Genomics and phylogenetics
Record sample-to-sequence linkage, accession, reference genome, database release, read-processing status, and metadata restrictions.


Model and simulation inputs
Record parameter version, units, scenario, initial conditions, boundary conditions, and calibration source.

title: Data Intake and Acceptance
text:
Intake completion gate

Authorization, owner, provider, restrictions, and access contact are recorded.
Project context, source ID, and snapshot/release/extraction/acquisition ID are assigned.
A separate intake ID is assigned when the delivery pattern or consequence makes it conditionally required; a simple one-time delivery may reuse its snapshot ID.
The delivered source package is preserved at an authoritative location.
Expected and received contents are compared.
Technical and initial content inspections are recorded.
Required metadata, identifiers, units, dates, geography, and domain fields are interpretable.
Discrepancies and clarifications are linked to the affected delivery.
Acceptance status and responsible decision-maker are recorded.
The data are explicitly received, pending validation, pending clarification, accepted for staging, accepted with documented limitation, rejected, or superseded.

Passing this gate allows an accepted delivery to enter the Organize stage. An accepted-for-staging delivery may proceed; an accepted-with-documented-limitation delivery may proceed only with that limitation carried forward; rejected or pending data must not proceed. Intake does not certify analytical validity, model suitability, publication readiness, or authorization for every downstream use.

title: Domain Guidance
text:
Future guidance will connect general research practices to the risks and conventions of spatial, epidemiological, ecological, genomic, and modeling work. Potential topics include coordinate reference systems, geocoding, case definitions, sampling and detection, genomic provenance, model checking, uncertainty, and responsible communication.
Domain pages should be developed with subject-matter review and should not be inferred from the resource catalog alone.

title: How to Use This Site
text:
Start with Start Here, then use the lifecycle pages in Research Practices and the domain index when a project has specialized needs.






Read the labels



Required, Recommended, and Optional describe the intended strength of a practice. Draft guidance signals material that has not been approved as lab policy. Example demonstrates a pattern without imposing it.


Pages include review metadata near the top. Use the repository actions to view or edit source, or report a problem. A page’s owner coordinates review; it is not automatically the sole author.

title: Contributing
text:
See CONTRIBUTING.md for the repository workflow. Propose changes on a branch, preserve metadata, write in your own words, cite the evidence or source basis, and request review when a change could affect a lab requirement.






Warning



Until governance is finalized, a pull request can improve draft text but cannot by itself turn it into an approved lab requirement.

text: Geographical epidemiology joins data, place, time, biology, and models. Small undocumented choices can change an analysis, while staff changes and long timelines can make a sound result difficult to recover.

title: Purpose of the Lab Book
text:
What this site is for
The Lab Book collects concise, reviewable guidance for planning, acquiring, organizing, analyzing, validating, collaborating, communicating, and preserving research. It points to templates and external resources without replacing primary methods papers, data-use agreements, or formal institutional policies. The Lab Book remains distinct from the GeoEpi organization website and GitHub organization.

title: Purpose of the Lab Book
text:
What this site is not
This is not a complete textbook, a substitute for scientific judgment, or an approved policy register. Requirements will be labeled and approved explicitly; until then, content is draft guidance.

title: GeoEpi Lab Book
text:
Draft guidance



The Lab Book is a living resource. Draft pages and proposed policy require review; they do not establish approved laboratory policy.
Welcome to the GeoEpi Lab Book, a shared place for practices that help geographical epidemiology remain understandable, defensible, reproducible, and transferable across people, projects, and time.

title: GeoEpi Lab Book
text:
Find your next step

Start a project for a minimum setup and scope.
Assess project readiness at lifecycle checkpoints.
Document incoming data with a source inventory.
Find a template for reusable project records.
Prepare a handoff before responsibility changes.

Resources for an annotated external catalog.

The intended outcome is that a lab member can join a project, understand what was done and why, reproduce an important result where access permits, identify uncertainty, and continue the work without relying on undocumented memory.

title: Acquire Data
text: Acquisition is more than downloading or receiving files. It includes authorization, specification, preservation, registration, initial inspection, clarification, and an explicit acceptance decision.

title: Acquire Data
text:
Acquisition workflow

Authorize the source, access, and intended use.
Specify expected files, tables, period, geography, format, and documentation.
Receive or extract into an approved intake location.
Preserve the delivered representation before correction or transformation.
Register project context, source, and snapshot identifiers; add a separate intake ID when the delivery pattern or consequence warrants it.
Validate enough to assess completeness and plausibility.
Clarify discrepancies with the provider or data owner.
Accept or reject for staging and further organization using an explicit status.

text:
Evidence and interpretation
The workflow draws on the existing resource catalog, especially RDMkit, DataONE, the FAIR Principles, CARE Principles, USDA NAL, CDC, FGDC, GBIF, EML, and EFI guidance. These sources support source preservation, provenance, metadata, access and governance, spatial documentation, epidemiological extraction context, ecological documentation, and versioned recurring data. title: Analysis Design
text: State what the analysis is intended to do. Useful categories include descriptive, comparative, explanatory, inferential, predictive, forecasting, decision-support, simulation, method development, and sensitivity analysis. Categories may overlap, but the intended use should be clear. “Fit a model” is a method description, not an analysis objective.

title: Analysis Design
text: State what the analysis is intended to do. Useful categories include descriptive, comparative, explanatory, inferential, predictive, forecasting, decision-support, simulation, method development, and sensitivity analysis. Categories may overlap, but the intended use should be clear. “Fit a model” is a method description, not an analysis objective.

title: Analysis Design
Analysis Design
text:
Identify the analysis data
Record the staged or derived dataset ID, dataset version, readiness status, readiness limitation, authoritative location, period represented, important restrictions, and analysis-specific subset. Do not rely only on an informal filename such as final_data.csv.

title: Analysis Design
Analysis Design
text:
Make decision timing visible
Distinguish decisions made before inspecting the outcome, during initial exploration, after preliminary results, after a failed or incomplete run, during sensitivity work, and during final reporting. Record the timing when it could affect how a later reader understands the analysis.

title: Analysis Design
text:
Proportional documentation

Small exploratory analysis
A clear notebook or script heading may be enough when it records the dataset version, short objective, settings, visible outputs, and a brief note on what changed. A rendered Quarto document or notebook may also serve as the run record when it contains the required execution details.


Publication-oriented or collaborative analysis
Use an analysis specification or equivalent, identify primary and secondary work, record revisions, name important outputs, and use result traceability where warranted. A separate specification is not required when a well-structured Quarto document, notebook, protocol, or README already contains the information.


Operational or high-consequence analysis
Use an explicit analysis version, responsible analyst and reviewer, controlled settings, identified runs, recorded failure and retry states, formal result tracing, and a readiness decision.

title: Analysis Design
text:
Stop and resolve
Pause execution when the dataset is not ready, the version is unclear, the target or unit of inference is undefined, a planned comparison cannot be computed, restrictions prevent the intended use, important settings exist only in an interactive workspace, exclusions are undocumented, or intended outputs cannot be identified.

title: Exploratory and Planned Analysis
text: Exploratory analysis is valuable. The problem is not exploration; the problem is presenting a decision made after viewing results as though it had been specified beforehand.

title: Exploratory and Planned Analysis
text:
Use clear labels

Exploratory: used to understand the data, generate ideas, or develop an approach.
Planned primary: the main analysis defined before examining its result.
Planned secondary: a supporting analysis defined in advance.
Sensitivity: examines how results change under alternative reasonable choices.
Post hoc: added after viewing earlier results.
Final reporting analysis: the version selected for reporting after the decision and review process is documented.

One project may legitimately contain all these types. The label describes when and why the work was done; it does not rank the value of the work.

title: Exploratory and Planned Analysis
text:
Record consequential changes
Record what changed, why it changed, who made or approved the change, when it changed, what earlier information influenced it, which analysis version it produced, and whether the classification changed. Examples include adding a nonlinear term after a plot, changing an exclusion rule, redefining a forecast target, changing the spatial unit, replacing a covariate, adding an interaction, increasing simulation duration, changing a scenario, or switching the primary result.
Do not require a formal change record for trivial wording, plotting, or formatting changes.

title: Exploratory and Planned Analysis
text:
Separate development from reporting
Use separate script sections, named analysis versions, separate exploratory outputs, a named final reporting run, and retained earlier candidate results when they influenced decisions. Do not overwrite the only copy of an earlier result, and do not prescribe one folder structure.

title: Exploratory and Planned Analysis
text:
Common failure modes

An exploratory analysis is later described as preplanned.
Multiple approaches were tried but only the preferred one is recorded.
A subgroup was selected because it produced a stronger result.
Changed exclusions are not reflected in the analysis plan.
Sensitivity work silently replaces the primary analysis.
A final figure cannot be linked to the analysis version that produced it.

title: Exploratory and Planned Analysis
text:
Checklist

Each important analysis has an exploratory, planned, sensitivity, post hoc, or final-reporting label.
Consequential changes after viewing results are recorded.
Planned primary work is distinguishable from supporting and exploratory work.
Earlier outputs that influenced decisions remain identifiable.
The label does not imply that validation has occurred.

title: Randomness, Scenarios, and Replicates
text:
A random seed is a recorded starting value used by software to reproduce a sequence of pseudo-random numbers.
A replicate is one repeated execution under the same general scenario, usually with a different random sequence.
A scenario is a defined set of assumptions, conditions, parameters, or interventions.
A parameter set is the recorded values used for one model or simulation.
A deterministic analysis is expected to return the same result from the same inputs and settings.
A stochastic analysis includes random variation and may produce different results across repetitions.

title: Randomness, Scenarios, and Replicates
text:
A random seed is a recorded starting value used by software to reproduce a sequence of pseudo-random numbers.
A replicate is one repeated execution under the same general scenario, usually with a different random sequence.
A scenario is a defined set of assumptions, conditions, parameters, or interventions.
A parameter set is the recorded values used for one model or simulation.
A deterministic analysis is expected to return the same result from the same inputs and settings.
A stochastic analysis includes random variation and may produce different results across repetitions.

title: Randomness, Scenarios, and Replicates
section: Seeds are necessary but not always sufficient
text:
Seeds are necessary but not always sufficient
Repeating a stochastic result may also depend on code version, dataset version, software version, random-number method, input ordering, number of parallel workers, task distribution, scenario ordering, and replicate ordering. Record what matters for the scientific work; a seed alone may not reconstruct a parallel analysis.

title: Randomness, Scenarios, and Replicates
text:
Record scenarios and replicates
For each scenario, record its ID, purpose, baseline or comparison status, parameter-set ID, initial and boundary conditions, intervention, start and end time, stopping rule, spatial extent, output summaries, and superseded scenario where applicable.
For repeated stochastic work, record replicate ID, scenario ID, run ID, seed or seed reference, status, completion, failure reason, output location, and whether the replicate was included in summaries. Do not silently remove failed replicates.

title: Randomness, Scenarios, and Replicates
text:
Bayesian and sampling-based analyses
Record chains and chain IDs, seeds, warm-up or burn-in length, retained iterations, thinning when used, initial-value method, software and version, and output location where applicable. Warm-up or burn-in means early sampling iterations discarded before results are retained. Do not assess convergence or sampling adequacy here; those judgments belong to future Validate.

title: Randomness, Scenarios, and Replicates
text:
Resampling and partitions
Record training and evaluation partitions, fold or resample IDs, random seed, grouping restrictions, spatial or temporal blocking, repeated partitions, and protections against data leakage, meaning information from evaluation data accidentally influencing model development or fitting. Do not interpret predictive performance here.

title: Randomness, Scenarios, and Replicates
text:
Simulations
Record scenario, parameter set, initial conditions, run duration, time step, intervention timing, replicate count, expected outputs, stopping conditions, failed or incomplete replicates, and the summary rule across replicates.

title: Randomness, Scenarios, and Replicates
text:
Common failure modes

One global seed is recorded but parallel replicates cannot be reconstructed.
Scenario labels change after results are produced.
Failed replicates are dropped without explanation.
Baseline and intervention scenarios use different input versions without documentation.
Replicate outputs are overwritten.
A deterministic analysis changes across identical reruns without explanation.
Calibration and evaluation simulations are mixed without clear labels.

title: Continuity, Onboarding, and Handoff
text: Give a new contributor the project purpose, current phase, authoritative locations, relevant data restrictions, current analysis and validation versions, active reviews, open decisions, expected next action, and contact for questions. Access should be granted through the approved system and limited to the person’s purpose.

title: Continuity, Onboarding, and Handoff
text: Give a new contributor the project purpose, current phase, authoritative locations, relevant data restrictions, current analysis and validation versions, active reviews, open decisions, expected next action, and contact for questions. Access should be granted through the approved system and limited to the person’s purpose.

title: Continuity, Onboarding, and Handoff
text:
Continuity
For work that is long-running, costly, operational, externally funded, or high-consequence, identify backup responsibility, current status location, principal workflow entry point, access owner, scheduled jobs or services, and conditions requiring coverage. Do not make a personal workspace the only place where critical context exists.

title: Continuity, Onboarding, and Handoff
text:
Temporary coverage
Temporary coverage records the coverage period, temporary responsible person, permitted decisions, workflows and deadlines, access scope, escalation route, and return or review date. It is not a permanent transfer of ownership.

title: Continuity, Onboarding, and Handoff
text:
Formal handoff
A formal handoff should identify outgoing and incoming responsibility, current analysis and validation versions, result IDs, repositories and data locations, reproduction steps, known issues and limitations, unfinished work, active reviewers, unresolved scientific or credit disagreements, partner obligations, accounts or services requiring transfer, access removal, and acceptance by the incoming owner. Clarify the current collaboration agreement and contribution record versions. A handoff is not complete until responsibility and access are accepted or limitations are recorded.

title: Continuity, Onboarding, and Handoff
text:
Contributor departure and offboarding
Preserve contribution history, update roles and responsibility records, transfer or remove access through the approved system, and transfer ownership of repositories, storage, workflows, service accounts, and scheduled jobs where applicable. Record unfinished work, partner obligations, credit implications, preserved records, and the authority for each change. Do not delete history merely because a contributor leaves.
Use the project handoff template when a separate record is warranted. Never include credentials; transfer access through the approved system.

title: Continuity, Onboarding, and Handoff
text:
Return and closeout
If a change to data, analysis, validation, or result is needed, record the required return to that lifecycle stage. Preserve the earlier records and identify replacement versions rather than silently overwriting them. Collaboration does not complete final preservation or records-retention decisions.

title: External Partners, Access, and Sharing
text: Identify organizations, partner contacts, responsibilities, consultation or review conditions, sharing restrictions, agreement references, and continuity contacts. Record references rather than copying protected terms or interpreting a contract. External agreements and community authority take precedence over this draft guidance.

title: External Partners, Access, and Sharing
text: Identify organizations, partner contacts, responsibilities, consultation or review conditions, sharing restrictions, agreement references, and continuity contacts. Record references rather than copying protected terms or interpreting a contract. External agreements and community authority take precedence over this draft guidance.

title: External Partners, Access, and Sharing
text:
Access follows authorization
Participation does not automatically grant access to every dataset, repository, system, credential, or protected output. Record who authorizes access, what purpose and scope apply, how access is transferred or removed, and which outputs may be shared. Never place credentials in a project record or repository.

title: External Partners, Access, and Sharing
text:
Consultation and decision authority
Distinguish partner consultation, required review, decision authority, and release authority. A partner may need to review a result or approve a use under an applicable agreement; documentation alone does not grant that authority or permission.

title: External Partners, Access, and Sharing
text:
Sharing and communication
Record restrictions, license or agreement references, confidentiality conditions, de-identification or aggregation expectations where applicable, and the intended communication product. Ready for communication means ready to begin coordinated preparation; it does not authorize public release, operational use, or unrestricted sharing.

title: External Partners, Access, and Sharing
section: Indigenous, Tribal, and community-governed data or knowledge
text:
Indigenous, Tribal, and community-governed data or knowledge
When data or knowledge is Indigenous, Tribal, or community-governed, the relevant community authority is substantive. Use the community’s own terminology and record who has authority over access, interpretation, reuse, location, attribution, and communication. Partners are not passive stakeholders: record collective benefit, responsibility, and the conditions under which knowledge may be represented or shared. Local authority and applicable agreements take precedence over this guidance; the CARE Principles for Indigenous Data Governance are a relevant governance lens, not a substitute for consent, agreement, or community decision-making. The resource is also recorded in the local resource catalog. Public availability does not override those conditions.

title: External Partners, Access, and Sharing
text:
Stop and resolve
Pause the affected work and record a responsible person and resolution when access authority is unclear; agreements are missing or incomplete; data or output reuse is unknown; consultation is being represented as approval; communication exceeds the agreed purpose; public repository exposure is possible; partner identity, responsibility, or continuity is unclear; community authority has not been established; or ownership of a repository, storage location, service, or scheduled workflow is unresolved.

title: Review, Feedback, and Disagreement
text: Name whether review is scientific, methodological, technical, data, validation, operational, governance, partner consultation, or communication preparation. Identify the object and version under review. A reviewer may provide important feedback without having final decision or release authority.

title: Review, Feedback, and Disagreement
text: Name whether review is scientific, methodological, technical, data, validation, operational, governance, partner consultation, or communication preparation. Identify the object and version under review. A reviewer may provide important feedback without having final decision or release authority.

title: Review, Feedback, and Disagreement
text:
Record feedback and response
For consequential feedback, retain the concern, evidence or reason, responsible person, response, decision owner, date, and affected version. Link the response to the changed analysis, validation record, result, or communication draft when applicable. Not every formatting comment needs a formal record.
Optional labels can make a record easier to scan: blocking concern, important correction, suggestion, question, or note. They are aids, not a mandatory workflow or bureaucracy. Record a response outcome using exactly one of: accepted and addressed, addressed differently, deferred, not accepted with rationale, transferred to another lifecycle stage, or unresolved. The durable project review record owns the response; resolving a comment is not approval.
A blocking concern may be overridden only by documented authority with a rationale and any resulting limitation. Changes to data or analysis return to Analyze; scientific support or validation concerns return to Validate; wording-only changes may remain in Collaborate or a future Communicate stage.
Independent review is proportionate, not universal. Consider it when choices are operationally consequential, discretionary, surprising or disputed, likely to be reused widely, span organizations, have high error costs, or were made by the decision owner. Independence may mean a different analyst, subject-matter expert, person, or organization; no universal count or separation rule applies.

title: Review, Feedback, and Disagreement
text:
Review is not approval
Review means that someone examined work for a defined purpose. Approval means that a person with relevant authority made a separate decision. Do not imply approval merely because comments were resolved or a reviewer participated.

title: Review, Feedback, and Disagreement
text:
Disagreement
Disagreement can remain visible without stopping all work. Record the positions, evidence, affected claim or decision, decision authority, interim limitation, and follow-up. If the disagreement concerns data, exclusions, model structure, or validation evidence, return to Analyze or Validate rather than silently resolving it in a communication product.

title: Review, Feedback, and Disagreement
text:
Checklist

Review purpose and object/version are clear.
Required reviewer or reviewer role is identified.
Consequential concerns and responses are durable.
Review is distinguished from final decision and approval.
Unresolved disagreement is visible.
Required return to Analyze or Validate is recorded.
Independent review is considered proportionately and its rationale is recorded where warranted.

title: Working Agreements and Shared Records
text: A working agreement records how contributors will coordinate shared work. It should reduce ambiguity, not prescribe unnecessary meetings or tools.

title: Working Agreements and Shared Records
text:
Record authoritative locations
Identify locations as applicable for project scope and status, source and staged data, analysis-ready data, code, configuration and parameters, analysis records, validation records, contributor records, decisions, current outputs, review comments, manuscript or report drafts, and operational products. Copies may exist, but the current authoritative version must be identifiable.

title: Working Agreements and Shared Records
text:
Durable versus temporary communication
Meetings, email, chat, and calls are useful for discussion. Consequential decisions should be summarized in a durable project location. A changed exclusion rule, data-sharing limitation, or blocking reviewer concern should remain linked to its response and final decision. Do not preserve every message or transcript by default.

title: Working Agreements and Shared Records
Working Agreements and Shared Records
text:
Change and review records
Record which version the team is reviewing, the requested change, responsible person, reviewer, decision owner, response, date, and affected analysis, validation, result, or communication version when consequential. A short durable summary is preferable to a long transcript that does not identify the decision.

title: Claims, Evidence, Uncertainty, and Limitations
text:
For consequential claims, identify the claim, proposed wording, claim type, supporting result IDs, validation record, scope, uncertainty, limitation, audience, and review status. A claim table is useful for conclusions, decisions, titles, abstracts, figures, maps, and public messages; it is not required for every sentence.
Use exactly these claim-review states: proposed, under review, accepted for current product, revision required, removed, and superseded. The safe default is proposed. Proposed claims are drafted but not accepted; under-review claims are being checked for wording, evidence, scope, uncertainty, or limitation; revision-required claims cannot be used as written; removed claims were intentionally removed and retain a reason when consequential; superseded claims identify a replacement claim ID or product version.
Accepted for current product means the claim was reviewed for the named product version and retains its supporting result IDs, validation-record ID, intended scope, uncertainty, limitation, responsible reviewer, and review date. It is not release approval.
Preserve claim type. An association is not automatically causal; a scenario is not automatically a forecast; a modeled quantity is not an observed fact; retrospective performance is not prospective performance; regional support is not site-level support; ranking is not calibrated probability; statistical significance is not practical importance; and support for one use does not imply support for broader uses.

title: Claims, Evidence, Uncertainty, and Limitations
text:
Scope and uncertainty
Retain the population or biological system, geography, time period, unit, spatial or temporal resolution, outcome definition, forecast horizon, data conditions, and scenario conditions that qualify the claim. Communicate uncertainty in a form appropriate to the audience: intervals, probability or scenario ranges, sensitivity results, qualitative cautions, uncertainty maps, or data-quality statements. Explain whether uncertainty changes direction, ranking, classification, threshold crossing, geographic extent, forecast warning, recommendation, or confidence in action. Do not include an interval without explaining what it represents.

title: Claims, Evidence, Uncertainty, and Limitations
text:
Limitations and return paths
Place limitations near the affected claim, not only in a final limitations section. State the consequence and downstream restriction. If a limitation changes data, methods, estimates, outputs, scientific support, interpretation, or validation, return to Analyze or Validate as appropriate. If it changes audience, partner conditions, contributors, or authority, return to Collaborate. Communication must not silently strengthen a result to make a product more persuasive.

title: Figures, Tables, Maps, and Accessibility
text: A polished figure is not proof of scientific quality. Link each consequential figure, table, or map to its result and validation records, check that numbers agree with text and supplements, and identify the exact product version.

title: Figures, Tables, Maps, and Accessibility
text:
Figures and tables
State the population, denominator, units, time period, data source, uncertainty, exclusions, and relevant limitation. Captions should explain what is shown and what is not shown. Tables should preserve meaningful precision and avoid implying more certainty than the analysis supports. Check labels, legends, rounding, ordering, color meaning, missing values, and source notes.

title: Figures, Tables, Maps, and Accessibility
text:
Maps
Record geography, boundaries and boundary date where relevant, spatial unit, denominator, time period, resolution, classification method, missing or suppressed areas, uncertainty, and the intended use. Do not let a smooth surface, color scale, or detailed basemap imply site-level support that was not validated. Do not expose restricted locations merely because a map is useful.

title: Figures, Tables, Maps, and Accessibility
text:
Accessibility
Useful alt text or an equivalent description should state what the display represents, the main pattern or conclusion, consequential exceptions, and uncertainty or limitation needed to interpret it. It does not need to enumerate every plotted value. Captions and alt text may serve different purposes; provide a data table or text alternative when exact values matter. Use readable labels, adequate contrast, patterns or annotations where color alone is insufficient, and a logical reading order. Consider WCAG 2.2 when a web product or applicable requirement calls for it; do not claim formal conformance without applicable testing. Formal conformance is not required for every internal document.
Review accessibility in proportion to audience, consequence, product, and channel. Record unresolved accessibility issues and who must address them before release.

title: Manuscripts, Reports, and Reporting Guidelines
text:
Choose reporting guidance based on study design, product, audience, field, journal, funder, or contract where applicable. The EQUATOR Network library is a starting point for health-research reporting guidelines. Examples may include STROBE or RECORD for observational or routinely collected data, TRIPOD+AI for prediction-model reporting, and STRESS for empirical simulation studies.
Record the selected guideline, version or access date, reason it fits, completed checklist or location, and unresolved items. Do not force one guideline on every project, copy a checklist into the Lab Book, or imply institutional adoption. A reporting checklist improves completeness of reporting; it does not validate a study, resolve authorship, grant release approval, or replace applicable journal, funder, institutional, legal, or community requirements.
Before release review, make sure manuscript, report, abstract, figures, tables, supplements, and availability statements use the same product, result, validation, contributor, and restriction versions. Peer review and release approval are separate decisions.

title: Research Practices
text:
The Lab Book organizes work around a lifecycle:
plan -> acquire -> organize -> analyze -> validate -> collaborate -> communicate -> preserve
Stages overlap and may repeat. A revised project plan can trigger new acquisition work; an intake discrepancy can require a scope decision. Each page distinguishes the Draft minimum, Conditionally required, Recommended, Stronger practice, Example, and Stop and resolve levels.
Plan, Acquire, Organize, Analyze, Validate, Collaborate, Communicate, and Preserve now have implemented draft guidance. Completing the lifecycle guidance does not mean that the Lab Book is institutionally approved policy.
flowchart LR
  plan[Plan] --> acquire[Acquire]
  acquire --> organize[Organize]
  organize --> analyze[Analyze]
  analyze --> validate[Validate]
  validate --> collaborate[Collaborate]
  collaborate --> communicate[Communicate]
  communicate --> preserve[Preserve]
  acquire -. revise .-> plan
  validate -. revise .-> plan

title: Research Practices
text:
Choose a starting point

Starting a new project for a short gateway and initiation checklist.
Plan a project when purpose, scope, roles, outputs, or completion criteria are unsettled.
Plan data management when access, storage, restrictions, identifiers, time, space, or computing need decisions.
Receive a one-time dataset when a file, archive, extract, sequence batch, raster, or field export arrives.
Design recurring or programmatic acquisition for APIs, databases, feeds, portals, and scheduled extracts.
Assess intake acceptance when deciding whether incoming data can enter the Organize stage.
Organize accepted data when a snapshot has passed intake and needs controlled structure, provenance, schema, identifier, spatial, temporal, and readiness checks.
Review analysis readiness before allowing a structurally documented dataset to enter Analyze.
Design an analysis when the question, target, data version, method, and intended outputs need to be made explicit.
Distinguish exploratory and planned work when decisions may have changed after seeing results.
Record an analysis execution for local, notebook, scheduled, or HPC work.
Trace a result when an estimate, figure, map, forecast, table, or simulation summary matters beyond a temporary exploration.
Plan validation when a candidate result needs a defined intended use, evidence, and reviewer.
Check assumptions and diagnostics when assessing how a method behaves for its stated use.
Validate a forecast when predictions, risk maps, or forecasts are part of the claim.
Assess sensitivity and uncertainty when reasonable choices or uncertainty could change interpretation or action.
Record a validation conclusion when evidence must be synthesized into a scoped decision.
Clarify roles and decisions when shared work needs clear responsibility and decision authority.
Establish a working agreement when contributors need shared locations, review, change, and access expectations.
Review shared work when feedback, responses, or disagreement could affect the project.
Record contributions and credit when contributors or expected outputs are changing.
Coordinate external partners when access, sharing, or partner review conditions apply.
Onboard or hand off responsibility when people, roles, or ownership change.
Choose a communication audience and product before drafting a consequential product.
Write claims linked to evidence when results need a defensible audience-facing interpretation.
Prepare figures, maps, and accessible alternatives for visual or public products.
Select reporting guidance for a manuscript, report, or model publication.
Prepare availability statements for data, code, software, or restricted inputs.
Review a release when an exact product version needs a release decision.
Record a correction or supersession when a released product changes.
Decide what to preserve when a project closes, pauses, or has a retention trigger.
Assemble a preservation package when records or artifacts need a durable, identifiable scope.
Select a repository before transferring a package.
Verify integrity and recovery after deposit and proportionately over time.
Preserve software and environments when future execution or interpretation matters.
Review access restrictions when governance, maintenance, migration, or deaccession changes.

The Lab Book separates draft policy, task guidance, templates, and examples. The Minimum GeoEpi Project Standard supplies the governing draft framework; these pages explain how to satisfy relevant information requirements without prescribing one folder tree, storage platform, workflow engine, or environment.

title: Organize Data
text:
Organization is not cosmetic file arrangement. It creates a controlled relationship among accepted source snapshots, preserved source packages, staged representations, derived datasets, schemas, identifiers, transformation records, QA evidence, and analysis-ready objects.
Each staged-dataset record begins as not ready for analysis. Its status changes only after the Organize gate has been reviewed. A ready status records the responsible decision-maker and decision time. Every new staged version requires its own readiness decision; superseding a dataset does not silently transfer readiness to its replacement.

title: Organize Data
text:
Organize boundary
The Organize stage begins after a snapshot is accepted for staging or accepted with documented limitation. It may include structural inspection, deterministic transformation, normalization, schema and identifier checks, unit and code harmonization, spatial and temporal standardization, documented exclusions and corrections, provenance records, and analysis-readiness checks.
It does not include statistical model selection, parameter estimation, hypothesis testing, interpretation, predictive-accuracy assessment, model-assumption validation, publication review, or operational release.

title: Organize Data
text:
Organize workflow

Confirm the accepted snapshot and intake status.
Register the working dataset and authoritative locations.
Establish project and data-object roles.
Preserve the source-to-staged boundary.
Transform source data through documented code or procedures.
Define identifiers, relationships, schema, units, and codes.
Establish spatial and temporal conventions.
Run structural and completeness checks.
Record limitations and unresolved discrepancies.
Approve or withhold analysis readiness.






flowchart TD
  accepted[Accepted snapshot] --> preserved[Preserved source package]
  preserved --> transformed[Scripted or documented transformation]
  transformed --> staged[Staged dataset]
  staged --> checks[Schema, identifier, spatial, temporal, and structural checks]
  checks --> ready[Analysis-ready dataset]
  checks -. unresolved .-> hold[Not ready; resolve or document limitation]






“Analysis-ready” is a workflow status, not a scientific endorsement. Passing intake allows a snapshot to enter staging. Passing the Organize gate allows a structurally documented dataset to enter Analyze. Neither gate establishes that a statistical method, model, inference, forecast, or scientific conclusion is valid.

title: Organize Data
text:
Evidence and interpretation
This draft workflow is informed by the existing resource catalog, including Good Enough Practices, The Turing Way, RDMkit, DataONE, TIER, FAIR Principles, FGDC, GBIF, CDC guidance, EML, and EFI. These sources inform practices for separation, scripting, provenance, identity, metadata, spatial and temporal meaning, and reproducibility. Access date: 2026-08-05. External guidance informs this draft workflow but does not establish GeoEpi or institutional policy.

title: Organize Data
text:
Analysis-readiness gate

The source and accepted snapshot are identifiable.
The preserved source package remains distinguishable from staged and derived objects.
Staged or derived dataset IDs and versions are assigned.
Consequential transformations are scripted or documented.
Code, configuration, and transformation records identify how the dataset was produced.
Corrections and exclusions are attributable.
Record counts and structural checks are plausible.
Primary, foreign, composite, spatial, and temporal identifiers are documented as applicable.
Duplicate and join behavior has been assessed.
Fields, types, units, categories, missingness, and derivations are documented.
Spatial reference, support, resolution, alignment, and boundary versions are documented where applicable.
Event, report, extraction, acquisition, processing, and aggregation times are distinguishable where applicable.
Restrictions and sensitive fields remain correctly handled.
Unresolved discrepancies and limitations are visible.
An authoritative analysis-ready object and responsible decision-maker are recorded.
Dataset status is explicitly recorded as ready for analysis, ready for analysis with documented limitation, or not ready for analysis.

Passing this gate establishes structural and documentary readiness only. Analytical validity, model suitability, inferential validity, predictive performance, and scientific interpretation belong to later stages. A ready status is therefore a workflow decision, not an endorsement of a scientific result.
Ready for analysis permits entry to Analyze. Ready for analysis with documented limitation permits entry with that limitation carried forward. Not ready for analysis does not permit entry. The Analyze stage ends at a future Validate stage; it does not establish that a method, model, prediction, or scientific conclusion is valid.

title: Source-to-Staged Data
text:
Before transformation, confirm the source ID, snapshot ID, intake or acceptance record, authoritative source-package location, restrictions, expected files or objects, documented acceptance limitations, and provider schema or documentation.
Do not transform a delivery marked received, pending validation, pending clarification, or rejected. A superseded delivery may be retained for provenance but must not silently become the current input.

title: Source-to-Staged Data
text:
Before transformation, confirm the source ID, snapshot ID, intake or acceptance record, authoritative source-package location, restrictions, expected files or objects, documented acceptance limitations, and provider schema or documentation.
Do not transform a delivery marked received, pending validation, pending clarification, or rejected. A superseded delivery may be retained for provenance but must not silently become the current input.

title: Source-to-Staged Data
text:
Preserve source immutability
Corrections, renaming, recoding, reprojection, reshaping, exclusions, and normalization belong in staged or derived objects. They must not silently alter the preserved source package. When physical immutability cannot be enforced, use procedural protection and a checksum or other integrity evidence when proportionate.

title: Source-to-Staged Data
text:
Transformation principles
Consequential transformations should be scripted when reasonable, ordered, attributable, repeatable, parameterized where appropriate, logged, linked to explicit inputs and outputs, safe from accidental overwrite, and deterministic when expected to be deterministic. No particular language or workflow engine is required.

title: Source-to-Staged Data
text:
Typical transformation sequence

Read the accepted source package.
Confirm expected source objects.
Normalize names and encodings.
Parse identifiers and date/time fields.
Standardize types, units, and codes.
Handle documented missing-value representations.
Apply explicit corrections or exclusions.
Transform spatial reference or geometry where needed.
Write a new staged object.
Run structural QA.
Record the transformation and status.

title: Source-to-Staged Data
text:
Corrections and exclusions
Distinguish provider-issued correction, documented local correction, harmonization, imputation, exclusion, aggregation, and derivation. Imputation or model-based correction is not routine staging and must not be hidden inside organization code.
For every local correction, record the affected object or record, original and corrected state where lawful and practical, reason, evidence, responsible person or process, date, and code or decision record.
Consequential exclusions must identify the rule, rationale, affected records, stage, recoverability, effect on record counts, and decision record when warranted. Do not allow undocumented row deletion.

title: Source-to-Staged Data
text:
Manual steps
A manual step is allowed only when scripting is not reasonable, the procedure and inputs/outputs are documented, the responsible person and date are recorded, the change can be reviewed, and the preserved source package is not silently modified. Link to the project exception record when a required traceable process cannot be followed.

title: Source-to-Staged Data
text:
Transformation record
Record transformation ID, input dataset and snapshot/version, input object, code or workflow entry point, code version, configuration version, command, output dataset/version/location, execution time, status, record counts where meaningful, corrections or exclusions, QA record, responsible role, and superseded output.
The transformation ledger template provides a compact format. Versioned scripts plus retained logs may satisfy the requirement in simple projects. A separate ledger is Conditionally required for multiple datasets, complex workflows, recurring transformations, handoffs, or consequential projects.

title: Source-to-Staged Data
text:
Version and overwrite safety
Recommended: write new output versions rather than silently replacing files, validate before replacing a current pointer, record supersession explicitly, and retain enough prior evidence to reproduce or explain a result.
Transformation statuses may be planned, running, completed, completed with limitation, failed, or superseded. These are workflow statuses, not institutional classifications.
Completed means that the documented transformation ran and produced its recorded output. It does not automatically mean ready for analysis. Transformation completion and the separate Organize readiness decision must remain distinguishable.

title: Source-to-Staged Data
text:
Structural QA after transformation
Check as appropriate that the output exists and is readable, expected schema is present, record counts are plausible, required identifiers are populated, unique keys are unique, joins have expected match rates, units and codes are known, missingness is characterized, expected temporal/spatial coverage is present, geometries or rasters are structurally valid, and the source package was not unexpectedly modified.






Stop and resolve



Pause analysis readiness when a transformation cannot be tied to an accepted snapshot, source objects changed unexpectedly, corrections cannot be explained, exclusions are undocumented, output counts are implausible, identifiers are unstable, join losses are unexplained, spatial or temporal support changed unintentionally, code/configuration versions cannot be recovered, or a manual step cannot be reviewed.

title: Plan Data Management
text: Data-management planning is a set of decisions that must be recorded, not necessarily a separate formal document. Reconcile anticipated information with the actual data-source inventory during intake.

title: Plan Data Management
text:
Anticipated data inventory
Before acquisition, record the source or provider, expected format, approximate volume, delivery frequency, temporal and spatial support, identifiers, update behavior, access conditions, likely sensitivity, and expected authoritative location.

title: Plan Data Management
text:
Access and governance
Identify the data owner, access contact, authorized users, data-use agreement, redistribution and publication restrictions, expiration or destruction requirements, sensitive locations, PII or linked identifiers, and Indigenous or community governance considerations where applicable.






Stop and resolve



Do not invent institutional classifications or assume that a storage platform is approved for every data class. Link unresolved questions about classification, storage, cloud services, backups, retention, PII, sensitive spatial data, and public repositories to Open Policy Decisions.

title: Plan Data Management
text:
Storage and authoritative copies
Distinguish the delivery location, preserved source copy, active working storage, derived-data storage, repository code and documentation, temporary computation, output storage, and archive or release location. GitHub is not the default location for large, restricted, or non-redistributable source data.

title: Plan Data Management
text:
Backup and recovery planning
Record the authoritative copy, backup responsibility, expected recovery path, consequences of loss, whether restoration has been tested, and whether the data can be reacquired. Do not invent a backup frequency; use the applicable institutional or agreement-based requirement.

title: Plan Data Management
text:
Identifiers and naming
Plan stable identifiers for the project, source dataset, source snapshot or release, derived dataset, model scenario, run, and output. Prefer identifiers that remain stable when filenames change. Do not prescribe one universal naming convention.

title: Plan Data Management
text:
Temporal conventions
Plan for event date, report date, extraction date, acquisition date, processing date, time zone, daylight-saving behavior, epidemiological week convention, and revision or late-reporting behavior.

title: Plan Data Management
text:
Spatial conventions
Plan for CRS and datum, units, geographic extent, spatial support, resolution, raster alignment, boundary source/version, and sensitive-coordinate handling.

title: Plan Data Management
text:
Computational planning
Anticipate the software stack, packages, GIS software, databases, command-line tools, containers, HPC, storage volume, memory, runtime, parallel execution, external services, and credentials. Dependency locking and containers are proportional practices, not universal requirements. Never place credentials in Git, README files, templates, or logs.

title: Plan Data Management
text:
Release and preservation planning
At initiation, identify likely publication repository, code release, data release or access statement, persistent identifier, archive, retention owner, and closeout trigger. Not all data must be made public; access restrictions and agreements control.

title: Plan Data Management
text:
Planning gate

Purpose and scope are recorded.
Responsible roles and decision authority are known.
Anticipated sources and restrictions are identified.
Authoritative locations and recovery responsibilities are planned.
Computing and external dependencies are plausible.
Expected outputs and acceptance criteria are stated.
Unresolved policy questions are visible.
A proportional README or charter exists.

Passing this gate means that data-management conditions are planned well enough to begin authorized acquisition. It does not accept any received dataset.

title: Define Project Scope and Responsibilities
text: State whether the project addresses a scientific question, operational objective, decision-support need, software or infrastructure objective, or training/demonstration purpose. “Build a model” and “analyze the data” describe techniques, not what the work is meant to accomplish.

title: Define Project Scope and Responsibilities
text: State whether the project addresses a scientific question, operational objective, decision-support need, software or infrastructure objective, or training/demonstration purpose. “Build a model” and “analyze the data” describe techniques, not what the work is meant to accomplish.

title: Define Project Scope and Responsibilities
section: Define the analytical or operational unit
text:
Define the analytical or operational unit
Record the population or system, geography, time period, outcome or response, unit of observation, unit of inference, intended comparison, intended users, and decision or publication context.






Example



A county-week disease model may use individual case records as inputs but make inference about county-week incidence. The scope should name both units so that data receipt, denominators, and completion criteria are not confused.

title: Define Project Scope and Responsibilities
text:
Set explicit boundaries
Document included work, excluded work, known dependencies, assumptions, unavailable data, activities deferred to later phases, and the scope-change process. Exclusions define the project as much as inclusions.

title: Define Project Scope and Responsibilities
text:
Define outputs
Distinguish internal analytical outputs, manuscript figures and tables, reusable datasets, software releases, operational products, dashboards, forecasts, reports, and archival packages. Every consequential output needs an authoritative location and responsible owner.






Example



A weekly raster workflow may be complete only when the expected dates and spatial coverage are present. “The script ran” is not the same completion criterion as “the weekly product is available for every planned region and week.”

title: Define Project Scope and Responsibilities
text:
Define completion and acceptance
Before methods are selected, record what counts as complete, which checks must pass, who reviews the result, what limitations are acceptable, and what would prevent release or operational use. Keep these as planned acceptance criteria; detailed analytical validation belongs to a later lifecycle stage.

title: Define Project Scope and Responsibilities
Define Project Scope and Responsibilities
text:
Determine the project profile








Profile
Planning depth
Review, environment, and handoff expectation

Publication-oriented collaborative project

Operational or high-consequence project
Formal ownership, dependencies, failure consequences, controlled outputs, and change authority
